title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: Benchmarks, Pricing and How to Use It
abstract: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full , its most capable models so far. Muse Wonder is a frontier model from Meta built for personal and professional AI agents. Both models target long-running agent work: coding, legal and finance tasks, and computer use. Muse Wonder is live now on the Meta Model API and Muse Code . Muse Wonder Full is limited to paid Muse Code plans. Muse Wonder follows Muse Spark on Meta’s scaling ladder. Meta team states that it was trained at its Prometheus data center , with gains across pretraining and reinforcement learning. Meta credits a larger base model for better results on unfamiliar tasks. Two named behaviors define the release: For developers, Muse Wonder plans long tasks and delegates to sub-agents. It also operates browsers, desktop and mobile apps. All scores below come from Meta’s published table at max reasoning effort. Several rows use third-party sources such as Artificial Analysis, Vals AI and Datacurve. Note: PSI, MemoryBench and FocusBench are internal Meta evaluations. The model card says competitor runs are best-effort and may not be tuned. SWE-Marathon results for rivals used Codex and Claude Code, so it is not a common-harness comparison. Step 1: Open dev.meta.ai. Click Start building to sign in. The Muse Code install command sits on the same page. Step 2: Pick your model. Muse Wonder costs $4 input, $0.20 cached and $20 output per million tokens. Muse Wonder Full needs a Muse Code plan : Power at $50 or Maximum at $200 per month. Step 3: Sign in with your Meta account. Confirm your name, accept the Model API terms, and click Get started . Step 4. Add billing, then create an API key. New accounts see a “No payment method” banner, and Create API key stays disabled. Add a card under Billing , then open API keys and select Create API key . Export it as MODEL_API_KEY , per the quickstart . Step 5. Test it in the Playground. Open Chat , pick muse-wonder-1.0 , and set temperature, max tokens and reasoning effort. Step 6. Copy working code. Click Get code for a curl or Python snippet. It calls the Responses endpoint at https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses . The API is OpenAI-compatible, so the OpenAI SDK works with a new base URL: Step 7: Or use Muse Code in your terminal. On Mac, install with curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash . On Windows, use irm https://dev.meta.ai/install.ps1 | iex . Run muse in your project folder, trust the workspace, and sign in. The default model is muse-spark-1.2 . Switch with /models , or launch with muse --model muse-wonder-1.0 . Check out the research blog , model card and developer docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: How to Use Meta’s Rebalancer for Task Placement & Optimization
abstract: In this tutorial, we implement the Rebalancer , Meta’s assignment solver, with a C++ core and a Python binding. We describe objects, containers, dimensions, scopes, and partitions, add constraints and goals, then choose local search or the exact mixed-integer solver HiGHS. We build a small datacenter, drain a busy host, and compare the two solvers on toy models, mutually exclusive hosts, synthetic clusters, and 60 published OR-Library instances. We judge every plan by recounting the returned assignment rather than by the solver’s flags. In this build, across 24 solves, the solved flag read True in 14 solves that still left memory over capacity. HARD under local search returned a violating start without raising; misspelled spec keys were ignored silently, and enum names are rejected. The timings come from an Apple M4 with the macOS wheel, and Colab’s Linux wheel may time differently. We install rebalancer 1.0.4 and print the Python version and hardware, because every timing depends on them. The binding rejects enum names and silently ignores unknown spec keys, so the notebook passes integers from one table and checks each spec before solving. A gate then solves a two-task model with both solvers, each moving one task, in 0.8 ms with local search and 0.9 ms with HiGHS. The cell also confirms that this build refuses the default XPRESS solver and the Gurobi package. We solve the README example, four 10 GB tasks on two 20 GB hosts with three tasks on one host, and recount the result instead of trusting the solver. Local search moves one task in 0.3 ms, and the recount drops the excess from 10 GB to 0. The solver’s own brokenCount also falls from 1 to 0 and endReason reads OPTIMAL. A control makes the point about the flag: with solveTime=0 the solver moves nothing, still leaves 10 GB over capacity, and reports solved=True. We build eight hosts in four racks, four jobs of four tasks each, and start with host0 at 200% CPU and 12 rack duplicates. We add CPU and memory capacity, a one-task-per-job-per-rack rule, and a CPU balance goal. The solver moves 13 tasks to leave two per host with no violations, with a median solve of 2.5 ms over three fresh builds. Without the rack rule, the recount finds 5 rack duplicates, and a RELATIVE limit on it also ends with 5, so it enforces nothing here. We test a fixable start F and an impossible start I under each constraint policy and both solvers, recounting every result. HARD with local search returns both starts untouched, with OPTIMAL and solved=True, while HiGHS fixes F and raises an infeasible error on I. Across the 24 solves, solved read True in 14 solves that still left memory over capacity. The solver’s brokenVal equals total excess divided by mean host capacity in all 15 samples. Read brokenCount or recount rather than trusting OPTIMAL. A lower goal tuple always decides first, and weights trade off only within one tuple. With both in tuple 0, weight 1 for affinity loses to weight 1000 for movement, and swapping the weights moves t0. With the affinity in tuple 0 and movement in tuple 1, t0 still moves. A fix-it goal in a later tuple than movement leaves 10 GB over with no move, while the reverse order repairs it with one move. The fix-it value is 10000 plus 100 times brokenVal, checked on two starts. We drain host1 under a ToFree constraint, leaving host0 alone in rack0 at 16 of 16 CPU. Unbudgeted, local search empties host1 in 13 moves with no violations, and three fresh builds agree. A stopAfterMoves budget gives a partial plan, not an error: at 12 moves one task still sits on host1, and at 6 moves the recount finds 4 CPU and 16 GB excess and 6 rack duplicates, yet solved is True. A misspelled key, stopAfterMove, is silently ignored, and the solve runs all 13 moves. We compare HiGHS with local search on balance, judged by recounted CPU spread, since objectives across formulas are not comparable. With the LINEAR formula, both reach zero spread, but local search moved 13 tasks in a median of 1.8 ms, while HiGHS moved 16 in 7.8 ms. IDEAL balances under local search but raises a HiGHS error. On three mutually exclusive hosts, local search stops with all three hosts in use and every conflicting pair still broken, because no single move lowers brokenVal. HiGHS clears the conflicts in 5.9 ms. We run synthetic clusters under a time cap, each in a fresh process. The 1,000-object, 100-container cluster took 1.22, 1.27 and 1.35 s across three processes, returned the same assignment each time and cleared all 13 overloaded containers. A 1,000-by-1,000 cluster took 3.55 s. At 10,000 objects on 100 containers, the 25 s cap is reached with HIT_TIME_LIMIT, so endReason and a recount tell finished plans from partial ones. Three HiGHS runs of the datacenter reach objective 0 with three different assignments, so we compare objectives, not assignments. We check the solvers against 60 OR-Library generalized-assignment instances with published optima, downloaded and checksum-checked at run time. HiGHS matches all 60 optima, every answer feasible, the slowest at 1.31 s. Local search from a first-fit start reaches the optimum on 4 of 60 even with the best of three seeds, and its best answer per instance falls 7.7 profit units (1.07%) short on average. Across nine runs, the mean shortfall ranged from 7.6 to 8.1, and even fixed seeds vary between runs, for a cause we did not isolate. We test bin packing with MinimizeContainers on two OR-Library instances and measure against the L1 lower bound, which equals their best-known bin counts of 48 and 20. Local search from first-fit decreasing removes no bin on either. Asking for exactly L1 bins with capacity alone packs u120_00 in 0.02 s, which meets the bound and so is optimal. On t60_00, local search finds no 20-bin packing, and HiGHS finds none within 10 s on either instance, which is a timeout, not a proof of infeasibility. The summary lists every claim with how it was checked, by recount, endReason or raised error, and solver seconds per step. In this run all 28 claims held and no step failed, with 90.1 s spent inside the solver. Not tested here are production scale, the paper’s or Meta’s latency and volume figures, and the XPRESS and Gurobi backends. Rebalancer turns placement into a readable model, solved by local search or the exact HiGHS solver. On these models it rebalanced an eight-host cluster across racks, drained a busy host, matched all 60 published OR-Library optima through HiGHS, and repaired a 1,000-object, 100-container cluster in about 1.3 s on the M4. The run also showed traps: solved and OPTIMAL can sit beside a violated constraint, HARD differs by solver, misspelled keys are ignored, enum names are rejected, IDEAL fails under HiGHS, and goal-tuple order decides whether a broken constraint gets fixed. Pass enums as integers, check spec keys, recount every result, and compare objectives rather than assignments. Check out the FULL CODES here . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: Few-Shot Text Classification with Scikit-LLM
abstract: Few-Shot Text Classification with Scikit-LLM Leveraging Scikit-LLM for one of the simplest yet most practical text classification tasks utilized in the modern AI landscape: few-shot classification. By Iván Palomares Carrascosa , KDnuggets Technical Content Specialist on October 14, 2026 in Language Models Introduction If you have worked with building text classification models, chances are you got familiar with the usual drill: collecting hundreds to thousands of labeled examples, cleaning the raw text, converting it to suitable numerical representations for machine learning models — like embeddings or TF-IDF — and training your model, such as a logistic regression or random forest classifier. However, when large language models (LLMs) came along, they changed the rules of the game — and that includes traditional machine learning pipelines to some extent. Now it is possible to classify a text by simply asking an LLM to do so. Here's the catch: shifting from classical machine learning workflows to prompt engineering can be challenging. Scikit-LLM is a Python library that bridges the gap between both worlds. It wraps the powerful capabilities of pre-trained LLMs behind the familiar scikit-learn interface — namely fit() and predict() . This article shows how to use Scikit-LLM for one of the simplest yet most practical text classification tasks in the modern AI landscape: few-shot classification, that is, classifying text based on a small number of labeled examples that guide the LLM on what to do and how. Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot Classification Before getting into our Python example, it's worth clarifying the difference between few-shot classification and another form of text classification that also gained popularity with the rise of LLMs: zero-shot classification . Zero-shot classification : The model is given a text together with a list of possible labels and asked to categorize the text under the most suitable one — all without any input-output examples. This paradigm relies entirely on the LLM's internal knowledge gained during pre-training. Few-shot classification : A small set of labeled examples, or "shots" (texts with associated class labels), is passed to the model before asking it to classify a new, unlabeled text. These domain-specific examples supplement the model's internal knowledge and better guide its reasoning. Few-shot classification is typically better than its zero-shot counterpart for highly domain-specific text classification tasks where texts contain specific jargon, edge cases, or nuanced sentiments. In most cases, providing just 3 to 5 labeled examples may suffice to "teach" a pre-trained LLM the extra rules it needs to perform a good classification — all without retraining the whole model. The good news: Scikit-LLM makes this process remarkably easy. Here's how it works. Running Few-Shot Classification with Scikit-LLM, Step by Step This example can be run entirely in a Google Colab notebook. It uses Groq 's LLM API, which provides access to free models. As a prerequisite, register on the Groq website and generate your own API key. Once generated, carefully copy your API key and paste it as a new "Secret" variable in Google Colab — found at the key icon on the left-hand side of Colab. Name the secret variable GROQ_API_KEY . After that, install Scikit-LLM as follows: !pip install scikit-llm -q While Scikit-LLM is built to operate with OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoints, Groq's API is among them. The following code retrieves your Groq API key and applies the necessary configuration to set up access to the endpoint. from google.colab import userdata from skllm.config import SKLLMConfig # Retrieve the API key securely from Google Colab Secrets groq_key = userdata.get('GROQ_API_KEY') # Point scikit-LLM to Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint SKLLMConfig.set_gpt_url("https://api.groq.com/openai/v1") SKLLMConfig.set_openai_key(groq_key) Next, we prepare the dataset. To use few-shot classification, we don't need a large labeled dataset as we would for training a new model from scratch. Instead, we need a small, representative set of labeled "few-shot" examples and their associated labels. Let's assume we want to classify IT support tickets into three categories. Following the classical machine learning convention, we name the few-shot examples and their labels X_train and y_train respectively. We also define X_test , which contains three unlabeled texts we want to classify: # Our "Few-Shot" examples to teach the model the nuances X_train = [ "My laptop screen is flickering heavily.", "I need a new mouse, the scroll wheel is broken.", "Excel keeps crashing every time I open a macro.", "How do I update to the latest version of Photoshop?", "I forgot my VPN password.", "Can you grant me admin rights to the shared drive?" ] y_train = [ "Hardware", "Hardware", "Software", "Software", "Access", "Access" ] # The unseen data we want to actually predict X_test = [ "The keyboard types double letters randomly.", "I am locked out of my email account.", "Zoom freezes when I share my screen." ] To use Scikit-LLM, we import the key class for our target task: FewShotGPTClassifier . This class wraps a compatible model of our choice — such as Groq's openai/gpt-oss-20b — inside a task-specific layer that lets us use it just like a classical machine learning model trained with scikit-learn . from skllm.models.gpt.classification.few_shot import FewShotGPTClassifier # Use a confirmed 2026 free-tier model on Groq, ensuring the custom_url:: prefix is present clf = FewShotGPTClassifier(model="custom_url::openai/gpt-oss-20b") # "Train" the model (constructs the few-shot prompt memory) clf.fit(X_train, y_train) Importantly, fit() does not perform actual training (weight updating) on the LLM. It simply builds a few-shot prompt memory for the model, containing the labeled examples it will rely on for reasoning and generating its responses. All it takes now is calling predict() to obtain predictions on our unlabeled text examples: # Generate predictions predictions = clf.predict(X_test) # Display the results for text, label in zip(X_test, predictions): print(f"Ticket: '{text}'\nPredicted Category: {label}\n") The classification labels the model assigns to these three support tickets are exactly what we'd expect — all three are correct: Ticket: 'The keyboard types double letters randomly.' Predicted Category: Hardware Ticket: 'I am locked out of my email account.' Predicted Category: Access Ticket: 'Zoom freezes when I share my screen.' Predicted Category: Software Wrapping Up This article has shown how Scikit-LLM's elegant design lets you turn pre-trained, open LLMs into machine learning engines capable of performing domain-specific tasks like few-shot classification. No heavy model retraining is required, and no large paid models are needed — just a handful of labeled examples is enough for the model to classify new texts accurately. Iván Palomares Carrascosa is a leader, writer, speaker, and adviser in AI, machine learning, deep learning & LLMs. He trains and guides others in harnessing AI in the real world. <= Previous post

title: 5 Fun Projects for LLM Inference Engineering
abstract: 5 Fun Projects for LLM Inference Engineering Want to understand what makes LLMs fast? Build the systems yourself. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 14, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Training large language models gets most of the attention, but once a model is trained, another engineering problem begins: how do you serve it quickly and efficiently? LLM inference engineering focuses on reducing latency, increasing throughput, lowering memory consumption, and getting more useful work from the available hardware. This involves techniques such as KV caching, continuous batching, quantization, prefix caching, speculative decoding, optimized attention kernels, and distributed inference. The best way to learn these concepts is not by reading about them individually — it is by building something and seeing what happens. In this article, we will look at 5 projects that progressively introduce the most important ideas behind modern LLM inference systems . 1. Building a Mini-vLLM From Scratch If you want one project that exposes you to almost the entire inference stack, this is probably the best place to start. Nano-vLLM is a small educational implementation of a vLLM -style inference engine, with its core implementation small enough to actually read. It includes scheduling, KV-cache block management, prefix caching, tensor parallelism, CUDA graphs, and other optimizations while using a real Qwen model. Instead of simply cloning it and running the example, rebuild one component at a time: first perform normal autoregressive generation, then add KV caching, then batching, then block-based KV-cache allocation. Benchmark tokens per second after every addition. By the end, you will understand concepts like PagedAttention and continuous batching in a much better way. 2. Writing Your Own FlashAttention Kernel With Triton A normal attention implementation uses large matrices and repeatedly moves data between GPU memory and fast on-chip memory. FlashAttention restructures the computation to reduce that memory traffic. Triton's official tutorial provides an implementation of a FlashAttention-style fused attention kernel, making it a great starting point for learning kernel-level optimization. This video also builds FlashAttention from scratch while explaining HBM versus SRAM, arithmetic intensity, tiling, online softmax, benchmarking, and finally integrating the kernel into an inference engine. I would recommend it to those who prefer video-based learning. This project teaches you that making an LLM faster is not always about doing fewer mathematical operations. Sometimes it is about moving less data . 3. Building an LLM Quantization Lab Take one small open model and run several versions — for example FP16, INT8, and 4-bit. Measure model size, peak memory, model-load time, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and quality on a small evaluation set. Hugging Face supports multiple quantization approaches, including AWQ, GPTQ, bitsandbytes-based 8-bit and 4-bit loading, and several newer formats. llama.cpp also supports a wide range of low-bit quantization formats and runs across CPUs, Apple Silicon, NVIDIA GPUs, and several other hardware backends. For an extra challenge, quantize both the weights and KV cache and see whether using fewer bits always improves latency or not. 4. Implementing Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding is one of the most enjoyable inference optimizations to implement. Instead of asking the expensive target model to generate every token sequentially, a smaller draft model proposes several candidate tokens. The target model then verifies those candidates together. Choose a small target/draft pair, implement normal autoregressive decoding as the baseline, and then build the draft-and-verify loop. Track not only tokens per second but also acceptance rate — which is the percentage of draft tokens accepted by the target model. Then experiment with drafting 2, 4, 6, or 8 tokens at a time. The Columbia high-performance machine learning project experiments with both speculative decoding and quantization using the Llama model family while evaluating latency, throughput, perplexity, and code-generation quality. An interesting extension is to test different workloads. Code, repetitive text, factual question-answering, and creative writing can produce very different draft acceptance behavior. 5. Building Your Own Production LLM Inference Service The final project is a capstone where we combine KV caching, quantization, batching, and benchmarking into a single system. Start with a basic OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint. Deploy it on a GPU. Add streaming. Add load testing. Instrument TTFT and token-generation latency. Introduce quantization. Experiment with speculative decoding. Add prefix caching. Push concurrency higher and identify what breaks first. The Time to First Token project provides an interesting structure for doing this. Its roadmap revolves around continuously improving one inference service rather than completing disconnected exercises. It covers deployment, instrumentation, heavy concurrency testing, quantization, speculative decoding, routing, and reproducible benchmarking. For an even harder extension, add a request router that decides which model or GPU should process each request based on queue length, expected generation length, or latency requirements. Wrapping Up You need enough machine learning knowledge to understand transformers and attention, but many of the hardest problems have surprisingly little to do with training models. They involve memory allocation, scheduling, batching, caching, kernel optimization, networking, load testing, and figuring out how to keep very expensive hardware busy. This is why building projects is such a good way to learn the field. Start by generating one token inefficiently. Add a KV cache. Batch several users together. Break the cache into pages. Quantize the weights. Let a smaller model speculate about future tokens. Write a GPU kernel. Then put everything behind an API and bombard it with requests. By the time you finish, tools such as vLLM and SGLang will no longer feel like black boxes. You will have built smaller versions of many of the ideas that make them fast. Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields. <= Previous post Next post =>

title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
abstract: Announcements Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore Oct 14, 2026 Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI. “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.” Supporting responsible AI in Singapore Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.” “Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.” Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil. Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models. We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index , and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI. How Singapore is working with Claude In our latest Economic Index , Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict. In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense. In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements. Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code. Building with the developer community This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers. Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders. Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our careers page .

title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
abstract: Policy Preparing for the 2026 US midterms Oct 14, 2026 Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards , which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information. Below, we outline how we’ve built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms. How people use Claude for elections and politics Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period. 1 Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase . This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude who or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations. 2 How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for. Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using a privacy-preserving method . Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies. What people ask Claude for in political conversations. Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through Anthropic Insights . Connecting people to trusted sources Ahead of Election Day, we've added two new ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works . These resources are standard across the industry.Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place can now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources. Official voting information presented by Democracy Works. Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation. Measuring and preventing political bias When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and even-handed answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are our most even-handed to date, scoring 99% on our political even-handedness evaluation . Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We’re continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics. As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies. The Future of Free Speech , an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the Foundation for American Innovation compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The Collective Intelligence Project surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles. These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email.And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.We’re addressing this in a few ways. We’ve improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We’re also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we’re continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we’re working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues. How we define misuse Our Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we announced last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don’t, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall. We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently published a guide to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent. Testing and strengthening our defenses We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse.

title: Agent observability on the Claude Platform
abstract: You can now send OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs to any OTel tool, and follow each step your agents take. If you already send Claude Code or Cowork traces to your observability tool, the agents you build on the Claude Platform can also show up in the same place. Trace agents with OpenTelemetry Trusting an agent with more access starts with tracing its model calls, tool use, and MCP server calls. Review its traces, then widen its access as it proves reliable. Add a destination in the Claude Console, and every agent turn, model call, and tool use arrives in your observability tool as a standard OpenTelemetry trace, with latency, tokens, and IDs. Works with your observability tools Claude traces follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions , so data from Claude and other providers works in the same tools and dashboards. Debug agents next to the rest of your stack . In Grafana Cloud , Honeycomb , Sentry , and Splunk , agent traces sit beside your logs and metrics, so you can see which service a slow or failed step came from. Improve agents with production data . With Arize AI , Braintrust , Datadog , Langfuse , LangSmith by LangChain , New Relic , and PostHog , you can turn real traces into evals, catch quality issues, and measure whether a change helped. Track usage across your organization . Send traces to Databricks Unity Gateway so platform and security teams can see token usage by team and flag unusual activity. Claude traces also work with any other OpenTelemetry tool that accepts a standard OTLP endpoint. Get started OpenTelemetry traces on the Claude Platform is available in public beta. Managed Agents and the Messages API need a destination in the Claude Console, while Claude SDKs export traces automatically. See the docs to get started. “At Foxglove, we’re building agents that help robotics teams debug their robots. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform lets us analyze agent interactions in PostHog alongside product usage data. That helps us evaluate how our agents perform in practice, identify where they fall short, and prioritize improvements for robotics teams.” Roman Shtylman, Co-Founder and CTO “Claude powers some of Ramp’s most capable internal and customer-facing agents. We built Reflect, an agentic system that scores their Langfuse traces, finds recurring failures, and proposes fixes. On some agents, we’ve already cut token usage by 10–20% and made sessions 30% faster. But Reflect can only improve what it observes. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude API can feed high-fidelity instrumentation directly into that improvement loop, with no extra steps.” David Traina, Senior Software Engineer “At Sterling Labs, we tune our systems like a race team tunes its engine. For agents analyzing live markets 24/7, Langfuse is our pit wall. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform streams every trace straight in with no custom instrumentation, so my team can focus on the edge, not the wiring.” Hyon Lee, CTO “Agents that touch a company’s books have to show their work, the same way an accountant does. title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms conference NeurIPS content type paper published October 2026 The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models Authors Louis Béthune, Victor Turrisi, Bruno Kacper Mlodozeniec†**, Pau Rodriguez Lopez, Lokesh Boominathan, Nikhil Bhendawade, Amitis Shidani, Joris Pelemans, Theo X. Olausson‡**, Devon Hjelm, Paul Dixon, João Monteiro, Pierre Ablin, Vishnu Banna, Arno Blaas, Nick Henderson, Kari Noriy, Dan Busbridge, Josh Susskind, Marco Cuturi, Irina Belousova, Luca Zappella, Russ Webb, Jason Ramapuram§** View publication Copy Bibtex Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities. † University of Cambridge ‡ MIT § Google DeepMind ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing content type paper published October 2026 Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models Authors Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter View publication Copy Bibtex Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora. title: Optimizing Agent Reliability and Tool Calling Efficiency for Chip Design Using NVIDIA NeMo Gym
abstract: AI agents offer remarkable productivity gains in complex chip design workflows, but their tendency to generate plausible yet incorrect artifacts makes reliability a major barrier to production adoption. In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation. Evaluating and refining these agents against verified final outputs, rather than isolated intermediate steps, is essential for building trustworthy automation. NVIDIA NeMo Gym , an open library for evaluating and improving models and agents using environments, addresses this challenge. The NeMo Gym agentic evaluation environment is designed to diagnose failure modes and track error propagation across complex, multistage workflows. By establishing a domain-specific verifier to inspect final outputs against verified reference artifacts, NeMo Gym enables engineers to trace complete rollout trajectories and identify root causes behind subtle errors. This post walks through how NeMo Gym was used to evaluate and improve the reliability of the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent when calling characterization tools. The Siemens Fuse team used NeMo Gym to scale up evaluations and verify the resulting Liberty (.lib) files against known references and tracing—both common and rare failures through each rollout. Those findings guided changes to the agent’s skill and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool descriptions, increasing the measured benchmark composite score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a benchmark of representative standard-cell characterization tasks, while reducing turns and output tokens. Siemens’ work provides a practical example for chip design teams and EDA developers on how to leverage the NVIDIA AI software stack and open libraries to improve agent reliability and chip design workflows. Automating standard-cell characterization Standard-cell characterization is the process of generating accurate timing, power, and noise models for logic cells across operating conditions. It is foundational to chip design and required whenever a semiconductor foundry issues a new process design kit (PDK). Each new PDK carries SPICE transistor models; design rules; and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) definitions that connect the manufacturing process to design tools. When a foundry updates a PDK, existing characterization datasets may no longer accurately describe the updated devices. Timing and power models must then be regenerated and validated for every affected cell across combinations of input slew, output load, and PVT conditions. The Solido Characterization Suite agent automates this process. The agent orchestrates tools from the broader Solido Characterization Suite through Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent, which exposes MCP servers and skills to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. MCP interfaces make these accelerated tools accessible to engineering agents, while skills guide their use in characterization workflows. Faster simulation helps agents complete engineering iterations sooner, while NVIDIA NeMo Gym helps developers measure and improve how reliably and efficiently agents orchestrate those tools. The Solido Characterization Suite agent must perform tool setup, large-scale SPICE simulation, distributed compute, Liberty file generation, debugging, and final validation (Figure 1). Errors often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures, leaving incorrect thresholds, missing corners, or incomplete cells hidden. Because these stages depended on one another, an early setup error could propagate into every step that followed. Defining a rigorous evaluation protocol was a key step in preparing the Solido Characterization Suite agent for production workflows. Figure 1. Agentic characterization workflow from SPICE inputs through pilot validation, scale-out, Liberty generation, and waveform comparison. Early setup errors propagate to the final library Measuring and improving agent reliability with NeMo Gym Part of the NVIDIA NeMo collection of open libraries for agent specialization and optimization, NeMo Gym integrates with the standard-cell characterization flow inside a controlled evaluation loop (Figure 2). It defines the task, tools, state, and verifier for each rollout so that attempts started from a clean state and produced comparable results. It also records thinking traces, input and output messages, and tool actions. This enabled engineers to run the following optimization loop: Run baseline rollouts with a versioned task and verifier in a custom NeMo Gym environment Inspect trajectories, failed tool calls, and verifier diagnostics Identify ambiguous instructions, unproductive actions, and incorrect tool selection Refine the agent’s skills and MCP tool descriptions Repeat the same tasks under the same evaluation conditions Compare verified outcomes and efficiency per successful result Figure 2. NeMo Gym checks the Liberty files produced by the Solido Characterization Suite agent and Solido tools, then feeds failure analysis into the next skill and tool-description revision. The entire process is driven by a coding agent with a human in the loop Reward design and artifact verification As the team analyzed agent trajectories, end-to-end evaluation uncovered failures that intermediate checks missed. For example, final Liberty verification exposed missing cells and operating conditions, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance. These findings show why engineering agents must be evaluated against final artifacts rather than individual tool calls. To make the work repeatable, the team implemented verifiers that provide a final composite reward score based on the following metrics: Coverage : Whether the agent produced every expected cell and PVT corner. Validity : Whether the delivered Liberty files are well-formed and usable by the validation tools. Relative validation: Whether the output introduced failures beyond those already present in the reference. Accuracy : The fraction of expected timing and power values that falls within the defined tolerance. Integrity : Whether the characterization workflow produced the complete result rather than reusing, truncating, or reformatting existing values. The reward score is defined as: \(R=\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Coverage}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Validity}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Relative Validation}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Integrity}\right]\times\frac{X_{\text{tol}}}{X_{\text{total}}}\) Here, \(X_{\mathrm{tol}}\) is the number of values in the output that are within tolerance, and \(X_{\mathrm{total}}\) is the total number of output values. Their ratio represents the fraction of output values within tolerance. Each indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals \(1\) when its corresponding gate passes and \(0\) when it fails. The reward is zero if any gate fails. Using this verifier, the team systematically evaluated and tuned the agent’s performance across multiple iterations. Optimizing the agent The team used the open source GF180MCU PDK to benchmark the Solido Characterization Suite agent on Liberty-file generation. The dataset includes 229 standard cells across 36 PVT corners, using Solido AFS for SPICE simulation. A custom agentic environment was built using NeMo Gym. For each run, the characterization flow was restricted to two cells across 36 PVT corners, as this smaller subset was sufficient for tuning the agentic workflow. Each run took approximately 1.5 to 2 hours, and the team conducted approximately 25 rollouts using Claude Opus 4.8 running in Claude Code as the fixed model and agent harness. Across successive evaluation rounds, the team refined the agent’s characterization skills and MCP tool descriptions.

title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors. In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can: Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges: An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration. In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents , an open source SDK for building AI agents. Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution. Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account. To deploy this solution, you must have: This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront ). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes. After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password. Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow. The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text: The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON: The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails : The vendor’s SKU format ( SB-004 ) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format ( AB-SB-004 ). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB- . On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds. When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow: The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting: The system improves over time through two feedback loops: When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation. You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py , so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own. Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context. The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example: To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/ for the implementation pattern. The agent prompts in agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/ reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt. Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system. Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The destroy.py script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store). To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources: Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev. In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning. To learn more about the services and patterns used in this post, refer to the following resources: For expert guidance on building document processing solutions, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners can help.

title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The supervisor agent exposes two tools: The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. The RAG pipeline works as follows: This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base. Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline. Guardrails operate at multiple stages: The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment. The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system. Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API. The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses. The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. Security measures include: Before deploying, you need the following tools and access configured in your environment: The setup process includes configuring deployment parameters and initializing the AWS CDK environment. Set awscliprofile to your AWS CLI profile name, or leave empty to use environment variable credentials. This creates the AWS CloudFormation CDKToolkit stack required for AWS CDK deployments. The deployment consists of three phases: building artifacts, deploying infrastructure, and deploying the AgentCore runtime agent. The build phase compiles application code and packages deployment artifacts. Run the build script: This compiles the .NET projects (Chat API) and packages them as Lambda deployment packages. It builds the PPTX Generator container image using Docker or Finch and authenticates with Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . It then pushes the container image and stores build artifacts in the asset-output directory. The infrastructure deployment creates AWS resources and configures service integrations. Run the deployment script: The deployment creates four AWS CloudFormation stacks in dependency order: After the infrastructure stacks are deployed, deploy the supervisor agent to AgentCore runtime: This script builds the supervisor agent container (ARM64), pushes it to Amazon ECR, creates the AgentCore runtime and endpoint, and updates the Systems Manager parameter with the endpoint Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The Chat API references this endpoint ARN to route requests to the agent. After deployment, AWS CloudFormation outputs include the Amazon API Gateway endpoint URL and resource identifiers. The solution offers several configuration points: Edit agent/app.py to modify the supervisor agent’s system prompt and behavior. The agent uses Strands Agents with two tools defined in agent/tools.py : In pipeline-params.ini , adjust model identifiers: With inference profiles instead of direct model IDs, requests draw on a broader multi-Region capacity pool, which increases throughput and helps maintain consistent performance under load.

title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest. The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code. On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub. Figure 2: Tamnoon AWS architecture Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something. It starts before any fix is even drafted. No remediation is written until an independent safety assessment, focused on scope and deliberately biased toward caution, concludes that the change is safe to make. From there, the platform draws a hard line between reading and writing. Investigation steps are validated as strictly read-only, so the work of understanding a problem can never alter it. Only the remediation path is allowed to change anything, and every change it makes carries its own backup, verification, and rollback steps.

title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region. In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration. Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps: This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments. UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio Code path using SageMaker Python SDK: UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio Code path using SageMaker Python SDK: This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload. Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications.

本次大會將集中開展行業模型、應用場景首發首秀，集中展示行業創新成果。 庫帕思將集中釋出建築、法律、金融、具身智慧、科學智慧五大方向行業標準，同步首次公開評測結果與榜單，為企業提供可直接參考的產品選型依據。 大會還將重磅釋出 “中國移動・時空智慧” 等熱點議題開展交流研討，分享工程實戰經驗與創業思考，帶來一場具備落地參考價值的技術路線思想碰撞。 亮點九：AI 工具現場實訓提效，人機共生共塑產業生態！ 當人類擁有軟硬體智慧體作為協作夥伴，人機之間如何開展組織分工？ 大會講壇、Workshop 等開發者活動，全面展現人機共生的新型生產模式。FDE 前線部署工程師，推動 AI 技術與千行百業開展廣泛落地與定製化對接。在組織智慧產業背景下，智慧體如同員工，擁有專屬 “身份標識”。人工智慧時代，探討如何帶領 AI “新同事” 協同工作。人機共生如何從理念轉化為組織實踐，答案或將在本次大會揭曉！ 亮點十：走進張江科學會堂，一站式配齊具身智慧 BOM 清單 200 餘家產業鏈企業齊聚大會，完整呈現具身智慧 BOM（物料清單），方案、技術資源可現場對接。 感知層面，自研晶片支撐
