title: A practical guide to real-time analytics in 2026
abstract: Data has always been central to business decision-making, and most analytical workloads aren't particularly latency-sensitive. But a growing set of use cases — real-time BI dashboards, operational monitoring, logging, live reporting — need insights that reflect what's happening right now. This is real-time analytics, and it's becoming a critical capability. "Real-time" can mean many things. Message buses move data between systems. Stream processors transform data as it arrives. Those systems are a part of most modern data architectures, and many are already sources of data in lakehouses and analytical engines today. The complexity compounds when it's time to actually query and analyze that data in real time — which usually means spinning up a specialized serving engine like Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, or ClickHouse, each with its own data copies, pipelines, and governance. That's a lot of overhead for what should be another analytical workload with a different latency profile. There's a better way. Real-time analytics should be a feature of the lakehouse where you already run your other analytical workloads . Learn what real-time analytics actually means, how to identify which workloads truly need it, and how a lakehouse approach delivers fast, governed, real-time insights without the architectural sprawl. Real-time data analytics enables organizations to analyze data and deliver insights with minimal delay after events occur. But "real-time" isn't a single requirement. A customer-facing recommendation engine and an executive dashboard both need current data, but they have very different expectations for speed and scale. Rather than treating real-time as a binary, it's more useful to evaluate workloads across three measurable dimensions. Freshness measures how recent your data is when it's queried: the time between when an event occurs and when it becomes available for analysis. A fraud detection system may need transactions available within a second. An operations dashboard refreshed every minute may still deliver timely, useful insights. Latency measures how quickly the system responds after a query is submitted. A dashboard might display data that's only seconds old, but if every query takes several seconds to return, users still won't experience real-time analytics. Low latency matters most for interactive dashboards, customer-facing applications, APIs, and AI agents. Concurrency measures how many users, applications, or processes can access data simultaneously without performance degrading. Internal BI tools may support hundreds of concurrent users. Customer-facing applications, embedded analytics, and AI agents can generate thousands of simultaneous requests. Together, these three dimensions define the requirements of any real-time workload and help you determine whether real-time capabilities are actually needed. The simplest way to think about it: does your workload need insights in milliseconds to seconds, or can it wait minutes to hours? Real-time analytics covers the first category — live dashboards, customer recommendations, operational monitoring, and logging. Batch analytics covers the second — historical reporting, forecasting, and scheduled analysis. Live BI dashboards, customer recommendations, operational monitoring, logging Higher performance requirements; demands low-latency serving Historical reporting, forecasting, financial close Most efficient, but insights are delayed If you run both — and most organizations do — you shouldn't need multiple tools, multiple governance models, and multiple security postures to do it. You should be able to run real-time and batch analytics from one place, on one copy of your data, with one set of controls. A simple qualification framework can help teams determine where real-time analytics delivers the most impact: The need for real-time analytics looks different across industries, but the underlying patterns are the same: organizations need to query and explore fresh data without the overhead of maintaining a separate real-time infrastructure alongside their existing analytics platform. Financial services. Faster analysis means less financial loss, and real-time risk visibility supports better decisions under pressure. Fraud detection, trading analytics, and risk monitoring demand millisecond-to-second latency with high concurrency across analysts, applications, and automated systems. Retail and ecommerce. Shoppers won't wait for yesterday's recommendations. Personalization, dynamic pricing, and inventory optimization need seconds-to-minutes freshness with high concurrency across customer-facing applications, translating directly to higher conversion rates and fewer stockouts. Manufacturing. Factory floors generate enormous volumes of sensor data, and the value drops fast. IoT monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational analytics depend on near real-time processing of high-volume data streams to catch equipment failures before they cause downtime. Healthcare. Delayed data can mean delayed interventions. Patient monitoring, operational analytics, and clinical insights require seconds-to-minutes latency with concurrent access across care teams and applications, supporting timely decisions that improve patient outcomes. Technology and SaaS. Product telemetry, customer analytics, and AI-powered features generate constant demand for fresh data at millisecond-to-second latency across large numbers of concurrent users. Companies that act on product signals in real time ship better features, resolve incidents faster, and deliver more responsive experiences. Organizations have typically met real-time needs by adding specialized serving layers alongside existing data platforms. These systems solve specific problems but create new ones: duplicated data, additional pipelines to maintain, fragmented governance, and operational overhead that grows with every new real-time workload. As real-time becomes core to everyday analytics and AI, this approach doesn't scale. Managing multiple copies of the same data across separate real-time systems like ClickHouse, StarRocks, Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, and SingleStore increases both complexity and cost. The lakehouse architecture combines the best elements of a data lake and a data warehouse to unify analytical workloads on a single, open foundation. By offering scalable storage, high-performance compute, open table formats, and centralized governance, organizations can support BI, data engineering, and AI workloads without maintaining separate data silos. The next evolution extends this foundation to real-time workloads natively, delivering millisecond performance and high concurrency directly from governed lakehouse data without requiring a separate serving layer. This means organizations can support real-time analytics alongside traditional data warehousing on the same platform, with the same governance, using the same data. On Databricks, Lakehouse//RT was built to close this gap. It's powered by Reyden , a purpose-built compute engine that enables real-time analytics performance directly on governed lakehouse data, with no separate serving layer required. In practice, this means a retail team can power real-time personalization from the same data their analysts use for weekly reporting. A financial services firm can run fraud detection queries alongside risk modeling without maintaining parallel infrastructure. And an AI agent can retrieve fresh, governed context in milliseconds from the same tables that feed the company's dashboards. Lakehouse//RT doesn't replace your existing Lakehouse setup . It extends it, giving you real-time capabilities on the data foundation you've already built. Separate serving layer (ClickHouse, Druid, etc.

title: Everyone's adopting AI agents. Almost no one can prove the ROI. Here's why
abstract: Amber Roberts, Staff Technical Marketing Manager at Databricks, has spent the last several years watching how AI actually gets used inside organizations, not just how it's pitched. In this conversation, she talks through why "faster" is the wrong way to think about agentic AI , why so many companies are struggling to show ROI on their AI investments, and what has to be true for an AI agent to be useful at work instead of just impressive in a demo. Most conversations about AI productivity are still about speed: doing the same tasks faster. Why is that the wrong lens for thinking about agentic AI, and what other KPIs should teams consider? Amber Roberts: Productivity is tied to whatever a team's actual KPIs are, and that's different depending on where you sit. For some teams, the work is detail-oriented and speed isn't the biggest issue. For others, latency is the whole ballgame. Even the word "speed" means different things: speed of development versus speed of inference, for example. Engineering productivity and marketing productivity aren't the same thing, and they shouldn't be measured the same way. So I'd push back on the idea that there's one right KPI to swap in. It depends on the team, and honestly, it depends on the person. Someone who's learning a domain from scratch is going to use AI differently, and value different things, than someone who already knows exactly what they want to build and just wants to automate the tedious parts. I'm skeptical of headlines that go all in on "this is the wrong way to think about it." There's a lot of gray areas. Even people on the same team can have different priorities for what they want out of AI, depending on their own expertise. There's a growing body of research showing companies are adopting AI fast but struggling to show real ROI. Why does that gap exist, and what does it reveal about how most organizations are deploying AI agents today? Amber Roberts: The people buying AI and the people using it day to day are often different people. The buyers don't want to be late to the game. Their job depends on staying at the cutting edge of technology, even if they're not the ones implementing it. If they see competitors buying and deploying AI, they're going to want to make a deal happen. That's true of any new technology: nobody wants to be the one left behind. Then, over six months to a few years, you start to see whether it actually built ROI, whether it was worth what was spent. That's the phase a lot of organizations are in right now: looking at what they bought, rolling it out broadly, and figuring out which use cases it's effective for. A lot of it is trial and error. But that trial and error is still better than being six months behind the competition. How do you define productivity in an agentic world, and how is that different from how enterprises have measured it for the last 20 years? Amber Roberts: The classic definition of productivity is how effectively inputs like labor, time, and capital turn into outputs like goods and services. What's interesting is that AI doesn't output a good, it outputs a service, optimizing something behind the scenes. The key shift is this: productivity used to be measured by how much work one person could do. Now it's how much work a person can do with a team of assistants at their disposal. We see this even in how we evaluate people, in interviews or take-home assessments. It's no longer impressive to see how much someone produced alone in four hours, because there's a visible difference between that and what someone produces when they're leveraging AI well. That's the new baseline. But it doesn't replace deep knowledge of the subject matter. It just means the same instinct, the same taste, the same expertise, is now applied at a different scale. Where I see the biggest jump is when people take everything that used to eat their day, the recurring, schedulable, "hire an assistant to do this" work, and automate it so they can focus on the harder, more creative parts of the job. The parts that require actual pushback and judgment, because AI's default mode is agreeable. It'll say "sounds good" to almost anything. That's useful for an assistant, but it's also exactly why the parts of a job that require someone to argue, to push back, to say "no, that's not right," matter more now, not less. That's also the part that gets missed when people report productivity gains without a quality metric attached. Productivity is technically linked to efficiency, and it assumes you're not sacrificing quality to get there. If a company says they're 40% more efficient, that's really only meaningful if quality held steady. Otherwise you might just be taking the same amount of time to produce the same result, with more moving parts. That tracks with what we're seeing in content specifically: when you push volume up, without extra attention to the details that make something good, quality tends to slip. The tools don't always keep up. A lot of AI tools can execute a task. What does it actually mean for an agent to "understand business context," and why does that matter more than speed? Amber Roberts: I think about it like comparing an AI agent to a real human assistant. If you ask an assistant to do something and they don't have your context, your schedule, or a sense of what's happened over the last few months, they can't do the job well. Imagine asking someone to plan an event with no guest list, no inventory, no record of what was done last time, what worked, what didn't, who the vendors are and what they specialize in. You can't just swap that out. That's exactly why people with deep institutional knowledge are so hard to replace: it's far more expensive to lose that person and train someone new than it is to keep them. That's where the value of business context comes in. You can get a lot of nice demos of "here's how you build this thing," with genuinely good generic instructions. But if you ask, "how do I build an addition onto my house," a generic AI tool will explain how additions generally work. It won't know your zip code, your local building codes, your city's ordinances. It has no information specific to your situation. And that's basically useless if what you're actually trying to build is something for your company, which is the entire reason you'd want AI at work in the first place. What are some examples of high-value, repeatable use cases emerging right now? Amber Roberts: Honestly, there are too many to point to one. Engineering is a good example: scheduling jobs, or using something like Genie Spaces so you don't have to be an engineer to understand the code, you can just type in a question and get slides, documentation, and context back, including who else in the organization is already working on the same problem. But it's really across every function: health, marketing, sales, finance. Every industry, and every team within it, has automated workflows that used to take a long time and don't anymore. It's a genuinely novel moment. There are opportunities that just haven't been touched or thought of yet, which makes this a pretty unique space to be working in right now. A concrete example: I recently had to step in for a colleague managing speaker confirmations ahead of a conference. The manual version of that process is emailing each speaker individually, or at best sending out a form and manually compiling responses. Instead, I set up an agent to message all the speakers, log their responses, and flag who hadn't confirmed. A second agent reviewed the outstanding responses and followed up automatically. By the time I checked in, all 137 speakers had been contacted and confirmed, aside from two who happened to be on parental leave. That's the kind of repeatable, cross-functional task that's ripe for this right now. How should enterprise leaders measure whether an agentic deployment is working?

title: What is HTAP? A plain-English guide to hybrid transactional/analytical processing
abstract: Consider a payment system processing a purchase. Before approving the transaction, a fraud model may need to evaluate it against the account's recent activity. But if that transactional data must first move from the transactional database to a data warehouse for analysis, even a short delay can make the result less useful. Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing (HTAP) brings transaction processing and analytics closer together to address this problem. An HTAP database lets you run analytical queries on operational data while it is still current, without waiting for a batch data pipeline to move it into a separate analytical system. In this guide, you'll learn how HTAP works, the architectural tradeoffs involved, and where it fits in a modern data architecture. You'll also see how different HTAP systems approach transactional and analytical workloads, how HTAP compares with Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing (LTAP), and what to consider when evaluating and adopting either approach. HTAP stands for Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing. Gartner coined the term in 2014 to describe architectures that bring online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together within an integrated database system. Gartner's original framing of hybrid transaction/analytical processing argued that combining the two would create opportunities for dramatic business innovation, because decisions could be OLTP handles high volumes of small, frequent transactional operations that keep applications running, such as creating an order, processing a payment, or updating an account. OLAP processes complex queries over large datasets to calculate metrics, identify patterns, and answer analytical questions.made on the latest transactions rather than on yesterday's extract. HTAP brings these workloads closer together, giving analytical queries access to current operational data without depending entirely on a separate batch ETL pipeline. For many operational analytics use cases, HTAP systems can reduce or remove the need for ETL processes, cut down the number of data copies teams maintain, and move closer to a single source of truth for both operational and analytical systems. In the most integrated designs, OLTP and OLAP capabilities live in a single system rather than in two products stitched together. Bringing OLTP and OLAP workloads closer together does not mean they have to run in exactly the same way. HTAP architectures therefore differ in how they combine OLTP and OLAP capabilities while preserving the characteristics each workload needs. Two common approaches are: A converged engine avoids the need to synchronize independent query engines, but it must prevent analytical operations from interfering with latency-sensitive transactions. A composed architecture provides greater freedom to optimize and isolate each workload, but it must coordinate data versions and keep the analytical path sufficiently fresh. In both cases, the central HTAP challenge is the same: provide analytical access to operational data quickly enough to be useful without compromising the performance and reliability of transactional workloads. OLTP and OLAP have different access patterns. Transactional queries typically read or update a small number of complete rows. OLTP databases therefore rely on row-based storage, selective indexes, efficient concurrency control, and predictable latency, often measured in milliseconds. Most transactional databases are relational databases tuned to keep that latency low even under heavy concurrency. Analytical queries, by contrast, often scan millions of rows across a subset of columns to calculate metrics or identify patterns. OLAP databases use columnar storage because a column store improves compression and reduces the amount of unnecessary data read during large scans and aggregations. OLAP systems can tolerate longer latency for complex queries, trading seconds of response time for the ability to analyze far more data. Optimizing OLTP and OLAP systems separately therefore made practical sense, but it introduced a new problem: the delay caused by data movement between them. Operational data typically had to be copied out of the OLTP system and into a data warehouse or other analytical database before it could be analyzed. Transactions and analytics processing ran on different schedules, on different hardware, against different copies of the data. Traditional architectures that separate OLTP and OLAP systems in this way build latency into every analytical answer. As requirements for fresher data grew, data teams started assembling their own custom systems to close the gap. Change data capture feeds, stream processors, cloud data warehouses, cloud data lakes, and real-time query layers became the building blocks of today's disaggregated data stack. Each component solved a specific problem, but every additional hop added cost, operational effort, and another place where data consistency could break. HTAP addresses that delay while preserving the performance benefits of workload-specific optimization. An HTAP architecture provides paths for both transactional and analytical workloads while keeping operational data available for analysis with minimal delay. The exact design varies by system, but the architecture generally includes transaction processing, analytical processing, workload-specific data representations, and a mechanism for keeping those representations synchronized, as shown below. The transactional path handles frequent application reads and writes, such as creating orders, updating accounts, or recording payments. These transactional workloads typically operate on small numbers of rows and require low latency, efficient concurrency control , and reliable transaction guarantees. HTAP systems commonly use row-oriented storage engines, indexes, caches, and a write-ahead log designed to serve these operational access patterns efficiently and durably. The analytical path handles analytical queries that scan, filter, join, and aggregate larger amounts of data. Columnar representations are commonly used because analytical queries often need a subset of columns across many rows, and they are what make fast OLAP queries possible on operational data. Depending on the HTAP design, analytical processing may run in the same database engine as transactions or on separate analytical compute. Separating the compute paths allows each workload to use execution resources optimized for its access patterns, so the system can add analytical capabilities without slowing OLTP systems down. Many HTAP systems also use intelligent query optimization, where the optimizer decides whether a query should read from the row store, the column store, or both. HTAP systems may maintain more than one representation of the same data. A row-oriented storage engine can serve transactional access while a columnar storage engine supports analytical scans and aggregations. These representations may exist within one database system or across separate transactional and analytical components. Some architectures also decouple compute from storage and use object storage alongside caches, logs, or other services. When transactional and analytical processing use different storage engines or components, committed changes need a path from the transactional side to the analytical side. Systems can use mechanisms such as change data capture (CDC), replication of the write-ahead log, shared logs, or shared storage to propagate those changes. The result is an analytical view that can incorporate recently committed transactions without requiring the traditional process of periodically extracting an entire dataset into a separate analytical system. How quickly those changes become visible depends on the architecture and its consistency guarantees. Bringing transactional and analytical workloads closer together introduces tradeoffs in how data is stored and processed.

title: OLTP vs. OLAP: Choosing Between Transactional and Analytical Databases
abstract: Online transaction processing (OLTP) handles high-volume, low-latency reads and writes against current transactional data, such as payments, orders, and inventory updates. Online analytical processing (OLAP) handles complex queries that scan, join, and aggregate large volumes of historical data across dimensions such as time, product, or location. Choose OLTP when the workload depends on fast, reliable database transactions. Choose OLAP when it depends on data analysis across current and historical data. As operational and analytical workloads move closer together, the OLTP vs. OLAP decision affects more than reporting. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents show why. An agent may persist session state in a transactional store while querying historical context from an analytical system. That setup makes freshness, data consistency, query breadth, and data movement part of the architecture decision. This article compares OLTP and OLAP systems across query patterns, data models, data storage, and latency, then shows how data pipelines, hybrid processing, and lakehouse architectures connect them so data teams can choose a better fit for the workload. OLAP and OLTP systems often handle the same data at different stages. OLTP systems generate business data as events happen; OLAP systems aggregate that data, often from multiple OLTP sources, for broader analysis. Take an e-commerce order. The checkout service must record it and update inventory without slowing the customer-facing transaction. That work belongs in OLTP because it changes current operational records. Later, an analyst might compare sales data across regions or examine buying patterns over several quarters. Those OLAP queries work across many records and group results by dimensions such as date or product. Insights can flow back, too: when an OLAP system reveals a recurring regional stockout, the team may change reorder rules in the OLTP system. Traditional architectures move those operational records into a separate OLAP data warehouse. How that transfer happens determines analytical freshness and pipeline complexity. Most organizations run OLTP and OLAP side by side, so the practical question is how the two connect. Online transaction processing (OLTP), sometimes called online transactional processing, describes data processing systems built to run many short, concurrent data transactions on current data. Online banking, airline reservations, e-commerce checkouts, and retail inventory updates all depend on OLTP databases because each transaction touches only a few records and must complete in milliseconds. OLTP is the preferred choice for applications that require high concurrency and strict data integrity. OLTP databases fit workloads where small, frequent changes must complete quickly without leaving the database in an invalid state. A payment or order update may touch only a few records, but each change has to be reliable. OLTP databases ensure data integrity through atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID) compliance. Atomicity prevents part of a transaction from being committed when another part fails. Consistency keeps each change within the rules defined for the database. Isolation controls what happens when multiple operations access the same records at once, which is how an OLTP database can enable multi-user access without corrupting records. Durability makes a committed change persistent, even after a failure. Together, these guarantees maintain data integrity and transactional integrity under heavy concurrent load. Most OLTP systems run on a relational database with normalized tables and row-oriented storage, both suited to write-heavy workloads and access to complete records. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle Database are common relational databases for transactional processing. OLTP data typically measures in gigabytes, although large production systems can grow well beyond that. Within Databricks, Lakebase is a fully managed Postgres database designed to support transactional applications alongside lakehouse data. OLAP (online analytical processing) describes systems built to analyze data at scale. OLAP systems prioritize read operations over write operations and run fewer but more complex read-only queries. Financial reporting, sales forecasting, customer behavior analysis, and business intelligence all rely on OLAP because they examine months or years of historical data rather than one current transaction. A common OLAP model separates measures from dimensions. Measures hold values such as revenue or cost; dimensions provide context such as time, product, or geography. These multidimensional data models let analysts compare quarterly revenue by region without working through individual transactions. Traditional multidimensional OLAP databases store data in a cube format, which organizes measures across dimensions and can precompute aggregated data for repeated queries. Modern OLAP platforms perform the same multidimensional analysis with denormalized structures and columnar storage instead of physical cubes, which keeps aggregation fast without rebuilding cubes each time the model changes. OLAP also supports data mining, complex data analysis, and complex analytical calculations that feed strategic decisions. Data analysts and data scientists depend on it for complex analysis, since a single OLAP database query may join and summarize billions of rows. Databricks SQL supports these analytical workloads with SQL warehouses for querying lakehouse data, dashboards, and reusable business metrics. Snowflake is another example, alongside other cloud data warehouse products and analytical engines. OLAP is closely tied to data warehousing. A data warehouse acts as a centralized data store that collects business data from multiple transactional databases, cleans it, and organizes it for analytical processing. OLAP workloads run in the data warehouse; the OLTP databases are where that data originates. OLTP optimizes frequent transactions on a small number of records. OLAP optimizes broad reads and aggregations that support complex queries. That split shapes query behavior, latency, data storage, and data management. The table below summarizes the key differences between OLTP and OLAP databases. A point lookup such as fetching a customer by ID touches a narrow slice of the database, which helps OLTP systems return application-facing requests quickly. An OLAP query may scan months of records before grouping and aggregating them. That heavier execution profile makes seconds or minutes acceptable for many analytical queries, and large batch processing jobs can run for hours, depending on the engine and data volume. Concurrency follows the same pattern. OLTP systems serve many brief transactions at once, while analytical engines spend more compute processing data for fewer, heavier queries. OLTP systems commonly use row-oriented storage because applications often read or update most of one record at a time. Indexes also help OLTP databases locate individual records quickly, although each additional index adds work to inserts and updates. OLAP systems commonly use columnar storage because analytical queries often need only a subset of fields across many records. A revenue report using date, region, and sales_amount can skip unrelated columns, so the engine reads less data as datasets grow. Columnar layouts also compress well because similar values sit together. Apache Parquet combines this layout with encoding and compression; on Databricks, it underlies Delta Lake for analytical reads. Data volume widens the difference, but size alone does not define OLTP or OLAP. OLTP systems focus on active operational records, while OLAP platforms retain years of historical data. At that scale, reducing scanned data matters as much as storage efficiency. OLTP favors normalized schemas so an update changes a value in one place instead of maintaining several copies.

title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
abstract: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)

title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
abstract: It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships. Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security. To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day.

title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
abstract: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
abstract: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it. This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded. Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs. Raising the red flag are researchers at White Circle, a public benefit corporation backed by senior leaders and researchers from Anthropic, DeepMind, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It was founded after CEO Denis Shilov posted one of the most famous universal jailbreaks of leading models in October 2024. Bent on breaking models to conduct thorough safety testing, White Circle helps companies detect and deter threats when implementing advanced AI systems that may not always behave as expected. Testing how well text-to-image models block banned content categories is a key research direction for White Circle, and Shilov thinks their latest findings are “horrifying” enough to share with the public. Simple to bypass In a little-noticed preprint published last month, White Circle researchers exposed flaws in the guardrails of DALL·E 3, Google’s Nano Banana 2, and GPT-Image-2. In a press release, they explained that “using just off-the-shelf tools, available online for anyone to download, and by sending API calls, White Circle was able to use the novel attack method to bypass the safety filters.” In the best case, on DALL·E 3, about 13 percent of the attack prompts produced images that human reviewers confirmed as explicit. The rate was under 10 percent for Nano Banana 2 and about 3 percent for GPT-Image-2.

title: The Safety Culture at the Labs is Broken
abstract: We need the frontier labs to have a deep and robust safety culture. Anthropic devotes considerable effort to cultivating and maintaining such a culture. It shows, especially among the members of technical staff. Having conversations with them can be a very different experience than talking to those at other labs, and there is a much greater sense of understanding and responsibility. But even there, the appreciation of the problems and their difficulties seem woefully insufficient. We see various symptoms of that more and more. Recently, while I’ve had some good interactions, I’ve also had interactions that make clear that much of Anthropic does not share that same safety culture, with a lot of ‘oh we will muddle through because we are better at operational excellence unlike those other idiots’ and a belief that all the problems are prosaic. Culture is hard. Then there are OpenAI’s cultural problems, which clearly run deeper. That point was only driven further home this week, with David Robinson resigning to blow the whistle, and OpenAI feeling forced to fire three of its safety researchers , on top of many past problems and incidents. That is on top of additional misalignment reports from both OpenAI and Anthropic. The reports are good things, but what is reported emphasizes that we have big problems that run deep. Thus, the growing consensus that we must find a way to Pace the Frontier and slow the pace of AI capabilities advances. This is potentially made more complicated by what could be increased competitiveness from Google and Meta, with the releases of Argon and Wonder. It is still too early to provide proper assessments there. There is a growing group of lab employees who have felt compelled to quit in protest. New York Magazine had a cover feature interviewing some prominent ones. The most famous is Coxon, who provided the tipping point for the current preference cascade. David Robinson became the latest researcher to resign from OpenAI and sound the alarm about the industry’s utterly irresponsible approach to safety. He also went on The Ezra Klein Show , which gives you a rich idea of where he is coming from. David Robinson was the lead writer for the Astra system card. That could help explain why he felt the OpenAI safety culture was broken. That card is screaming that things are horribly wrong, for those with ears to hear. David is not even that worried about existential risk. His worries are mundane, and he realizes that even on that level OpenAI’s safety culture is deeply broken. As always, we deeply thank him for sounding the alarm. I hope to write his name in these posts many times over the coming months and years. When you have to open your whistleblowing essay about the lack of safety at OpenAI saying it has become a cliche to blow the whistle on the utter lack of safety at OpenAI, there might be a problem with the lack of safety at OpenAI. David Robinson : What I’m about to tell you has, I realize, become something of a cliché: I resigned this week from OpenAI. I led the writing of the safety reports we published with each major launch. Now I’m joining a parade of former colleagues—at OpenAI and the industry’s other leaders—who have decided that the current path is unacceptable. I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture. We have to look at rules, and at laws, and also at culture. The more I thought about various potential laws and regulations, or safety and security plans or other commitments, the more I concluded that without a strong safety culture, and without the spirit of the rules, there is no hope. You cannot, in any reasonable way, have rules that cannot be gamed by those determined to game them. Two changes are urgently needed. First: AI companies need to rely more on the safety expertise that already exists in other fields. And second, before we create systems significantly more capable than the ones we have today, we need new science to ensure that more capable models (and their successors) will make safe choices when we aren’t looking. Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. Even though, as I detail later, David Robinson is not on the existential risk train, he still understands that alignment is a science problem, and we will need new science. ‘Oh it will not kill literally everyone,’ even if it were true, would not be an excuse to not do the safety work. It should be hard to argue with either of those suggestions. And yet. We have experts in mundane safety and solving prosaic issues. OpenAI does not hire them, and neither to my knowledge do Anthropic or Google or anyone else. After three and a half years at OpenAI, I was among the longest-tenured employees at the company. I led the drafting of our current Preparedness Framework, and oversaw the writing of safety reports on 12 frontier launches. But as far as I know, I never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing. To be clear, this is a new need: Today and tomorrow’s AI systems are far more capable and dangerous than the systems we were building even six months ago. I disagree only with the final sentence. This is not a new need. You need to prepare for the future, not only for the present. Even setting that aside, mundane safety issues have been crippling AI’s potential utility for years. This is a slam dunk thing to do. Miles Brundage : David’s right. I regret helping spread the idea of “iterative deployment” which maybe briefly made sense in the GPT-3 era but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks. The industry needs to mature ASAP. Elaborating on iterative deployment – obviously you should learn from experience the things that can’t be learned without experience. The issue is when you ship things with *already-known* flaws, in a way that doesn’t actually speed up learning but just speeds up shipping. … Also, as usual it bears repeating that this is not just an OpenAI issue. roon (OpenAI): you shouldn’t regret it. iterative deployment was a massive success. if we’ve now learned that it’s too dangerous to scale much further, we will have learned that lesson thanks to the process of iterative deployment Miles Brundage : So I think part of the issue is people mean tons of different things by it lol if it just means “don’t sit on stuff forever/get some real world experience,” sure, no regrets. It’s the “giving license to sloppiness” part that I should have realized would happen w/ that term. Michael Caley : this is by far the best “I quit my AI job over safety concerns” essay yet because it is the first one that talks about safety concerns in practical terms and that understands “safety” as a topic with extensive literature and best practices in analogous fields Joshua Achiam (OpenAI): David’s critique is substantive and deserves careful consideration. My impression of David from our time overlapping at OpenAI is of a sober and thoughtful person who didn’t approach the work from an ideological lens. This isn’t someone who came in with pre-formed opinions about existential risk; he wasn’t to my knowledge an EA. He was consistently productive, collaborative, and well-reasoned in his approach to safety. The core of his critique – that professional safety engineering practices from other fields haven’t taken enough root in AI safety – is substantial and correct.

title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
abstract: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA. The Kaggle competition : about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete. Clever Hans in ChEMBL : models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does. Hermes , trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB. Breaking the pocket : engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites. Lumacaftor -like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins. The agent sandbox : LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100. The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme. The Kosuri paradox : if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets. What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification. The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet. As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

title: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks
abstract: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench , simply independently confirm their claims. About 20,000 joined AIE NYC today for keynotes from the frontier of AI x Finance, from Anthropic showing how they are building the modern AI Financial Services stack , Vals AI CEO discussing their principles behind benchmarking models like Argon, and Coatue’s Head of AI showing how they turn news into investment decisions. All keynotes are transcribed here and all talks/workshops will be released ASAP. Tune in tomorrow for Day 3: AI News for 10/12/2026-10/13/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Frontier Model Launches: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Gemini 4 Argon : Google released Argon globally for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber defense. Access spans the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform; Google AI Pro and Ultra in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search; and Ultra in Antigravity. The official rollout supersedes an earlier newsletter claim that access was restricted to cybersecurity defenders ( announcement ). Pricing : Introductory API rates are $2/$10 per million input/output tokens , with cached input discounted 95%. Artificial Analysis reports that rates double to $4/$20 after November 30 —an important qualification for cost comparisons ( Google pricing , discount schedule ). Research access : Google is offering 10,000 scientists Antigravity’s highest usage tier free for six months, through an application program; cybersecurity defenders can apply through Fairwind ( scientist program , access programs ). Google’s internal results : Google says Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six-million-line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes. It also reports 35% more agentic code submissions , with rollbacks reduced by nearly one-third. These are internal deployment claims, not controlled productivity measurements ( engineering results ). Physical-task demonstration : DeepMind researchers describe Argon deriving a cornhole simulation from human video, performing system identification and refining throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot before achieving seven consecutive successful throws. Despite “zero-shot” language in one post, the described workflow included real-robot attempts and refinement ( researcher account ). Developer distribution : Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort , on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 ( Cursor , Devin , Copilot ). App integration : Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify ( coding interface , connected apps ). Muse Wonder’s positioning : Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case ( capability discussion , Meta positioning ). Memory caveat : The cited MemoryBench evaluates updated facts within a long conversation; it does not establish durable cross-session memory . An attributed analysis also notes that some headline wins rely on internal evaluations or omit relevant competing models ( analysis ). Muse rollout and economics : Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison ( pricing complaint , weekly allowance ). Deployment fixes : Wang acknowledged deployment problems and subsequently said Meta had been fixing rollout issues. Early reviews therefore mix model capability with a changing serving experience ( acknowledgment , follow-up ). Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World Reliability Argon’s capability–cost position : Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index ( evaluation ). Metric interpretation : AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. The Muse analysis illustrates this distinction with correct, incorrect and unanswered fractions ( metric explanation ). Agent leaderboard : Arena places Argon High fifth, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra at Max effort. Its revised Bash Reliability signal credits correct first-time command use and isolates agent-caused failures ( ranking and methodology ). Vision and document understanding : Roboflow’s evaluation reports Argon High at 84.7% text localization/recognition versus Astra’s 76.8%, and 85.1% object detection versus 83.6%. It reports roughly fourfold lower cost and latency of 19.6 versus 29.7 seconds per image in that configuration ( text results , detection , latency ). Document-specific evidence : LlamaIndex finds Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder strong on hard document OCR, highlighting table understanding at their respective price points and competitive chart, reading-order and formatting recognition ( document evaluation ). Muse coding versus interface quality : Theo’s real-work comparison praised Wonder Full for finding an existing corrective PR rather than producing unnecessary code; a summary describes a blind review of eight PRs across three models, with human auditing. Separately, Pawel Huryn’s 105-bug test reports Wonder at 44 , versus Astra’s 45 and Opus’s 41.7 ( original comparison , review methodology summary , bug test ). Competing UI measurements : Theo judged Wonder poor at UI generation. Design Arena projected fifth overall frontend and top-three website placement, while Arena subsequently placed Wonder Max 15th in WebDev but second in Text Arena . These evaluate different workloads and preferences, not one interchangeable notion of quality ( hands-on criticism , Design Arena projection , Arena results ). Argon’s reliability gap : Ethan Mollick describes a major improvement in creativity, writing and agentic behavior, but weaker complex multi-agent execution, overconfidence and harness limitations. Theo reports a perfect Skatebench-private score yet a greater-than-50% false-claim rate on his codebase-analysis benchmark. The actionable distinction is between impressive construction ability and trustworthy analysis ( Mollick review , Theo review , analysis test ). Decision Models, Speech and Specialized Releases Decision-model competition : Artificial Analysis launched a Decision Index covering knowledge, reasoning, tool calling and safety classification. Jev 1.13 leads its published decision-model results at 58; Haiku 5.5 Low scores 61 but costs $184 versus $42 per million tasks and takes 1.4 versus 0.13 seconds per task . Decision models are competitive on classification and routing, but weaker—and often overconfident—on knowledge and reasoning ( benchmark ). ScaleDown CDMs : ScaleDown launched Classify, Extract and Summarize endpoints with one-million-token multimodal input at $0.05 per million input tokens , with free output. Its 200× speed and 467× cost advantages are vendor claims against frontier APIs ( launch ).

title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
abstract: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month! This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube . Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2 , a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude . They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1 , that has to be seen to be believed: In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy , and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack. From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung , Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason’s journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna. to Founding Dyna Robotics 01:04:20 Dyna’s Research Culture and the Future of Robotics Swyx [00:00:00]: All right, we’re here on site with Jason Ma, the co-founder, chief scientist of Dyna Robotics. Thanks for having us in your office. Jason Ma [00:00:06]: Of course. Thank you for coming. Vibhu [00:00:07]: It’s been a blast. We got to see—you’ll see plenty of B-roll—drinks being pulled, a lot of evals, robots with knives for the first time. So under the hood of all this you have a world action model. What is that? Jason Ma [00:00:22]: So last month, we released our world action model called Dyna-2. So it’s the first world action model trained on more than one million hours of data. So going back to your question first, world action model is a model that’s able to predict the future video, the future state of the world, so hence the name world model. But in addition, you can also use that future generation to also produce actions robots can execute in the physical world to control the robot. So why do we do that? It’s a very powerful architecture, because if you think about how humans act in the physical world, in our brain, we are implicitly thinking about how the world will evolve based on our actions. So now we have a model architecture that’s able to do that to guide robot actions. So what we find is that by doing so, the model is much more dexterous, much more robust, and much more capable of generalizing to environments, to scenarios it’s never seen before. Vibhu [00:01:17]: I wanna prompt this question a bit. I think a lot of people hear world model, and they think you’re outputting video or world or 3D state. You’re also doing action. I think most people don’t understand what models are under the hood of robotics. So what are the inputs and outputs? What’s the training data? What is the architecture? Give us all the details. Jason Ma [00:01:39]: So, for inputs, the most important input is video, right? You can think about videos that the robot is capturing with its cameras, right? So video or images of the past many seconds, that’s the input. But for robots, what’s really interesting is that robot also has a lot of actuators and joint encoders on itself. So the robot also knows, the angles of its joints. So those can also be inputs to this world model. That’s something that’s very different from just a pure video model that’s only looking at videos, right? So that’s the input. And additionally, for robots, you want to be able to talk to it, to instruct it to do different tasks, right? So you can also feed it language instruction. So those are what I consider the basic set of inputs that go into any robotics models, including world action models. And once we have that the output, at the basic level, it needs to output actions the robots can execute on the hardware. But in the case of world action model, what’s really interesting is that in addition to the actions, it can also output future video, right? So basically, you can almost output the future video or some representation of it first, and then use that to guide robot actions. So the way I think about it is this is kind of analogous to chain of thought, you know. And basically, the models are reasoning in the visual, the physics space, and then outputting actions. So that’s the key difference between world action models outputs versus other kind of models, robot models outputs. Vibhu [00:03:08]: You put out a good blog post around your model. I think a lot of people understand language models or transformers, next-token predictors. In this case, you shared quite a bit.
