title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
abstract: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub:  https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony  Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

title: Anthropic conjures threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse
abstract:
ai and ml Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse Self-replicating AI botnets could become feasible on IoT hardware within months, claims the Claude maker, if smaller models get smarter Brandon Vigliarolo Brandon Vigliarolo GOVERNMENT AND IT NEWS REPORTER Published tue 13 Oct 2026 // 17:49 UTC READ MORE Security researchers spent 6 days doing their Chromework, built 1B user exploit now Ivanti patches Connect Secure zero-day after researchers confirm in-the-wild attacks 1 hour ago OpenAI engineer charged after boardroom bug found wrapped in toilet paper 9 hours ago Ransomware gets personal: 'We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff' 14 hours ago Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code 20 hours ago Nothing sells AI products as well as fear. Using new research, Anthropic claims that self-replicating AI worms could be just months away from spreading across vulnerable IoT devices, which would be a problem if it came true. The frontier lab published a research report Monday suggesting that AI models could eventually self-replicate without relying on datacenter hardware, with a 9-billion-parameter model successfully setting up inference on eight of the nine hardware types Anthropic tested. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” Anthropic warned, adding that such an AI worm could also suss out the workings of unfamiliar devices, potentially making it more adaptable than conventional botnets like Mirai , Kimwolf (the representative IoT botnet threat model used in the study), and others. REG AD Anthropic’s researchers managed to get a distributed instance of Gemma4-26B-A4B running across 15 generic Android set-top streaming boxes - a common target of traditional botnet malware due to their lax security. Once up and running, the distributed Gemma4 model was able to conduct inference tasks at a blistering 0.39 tokens per second. REG AD That, says Anthropic, proves that AI models can conduct inference with their various layers distributed across cheap hardware, but it doesn't prove such a model could self-replicate. For that, the researchers turned to Z.ai’s GLM 5.2. GLM was used to propagate a copy of Llama3.1-8B across eight Google Cloud instances running an Android 15 emulator in a virtual private cloud, which Anthropic said it was able to do with a high degree of success, with the model successfully spreading to all eight nodes in four out of five trials, and seven of eight in the other. “It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process,” Anthropic explained. Sanity check: This isn’t going to end the world, either Frontier AI labs have become adept at publishing findings that portend doom that only they can prevent . Doing more than a cursory reading of this report suggests that this threat is just as deserving of a big, honking asterisk as the rest. Take, for example, what is needed for an AI model to exploit vulnerabilities and spread to various systems. One would think that such an element would be an important part of demonstrating the danger of a self-replicating AI botnet, but Anthropic decided it didn’t need to worry about that for this study. “We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process, since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools,” Anthropic explained in the writeup. In other words, the replication these models managed to achieve was done on nodes that were custom-built for this project and deliberately left open to attack, although the draggingly slow inference demonstration ran on real, inexpensive Android TV boxes. As Anthropic notes, AI models can also benefit from being given the right tools to turn them into capable cyberattack agents. There was a custom-built harness called Memento involved in this scenario too. REG AD Are IoT nodes that get hijacked by botnets famously insecure? Yes, but it doesn’t take much to prevent the most common ingress routes – that’s just good security hygiene that has nothing to do with the involvement of AI. Anthropic acknowledged that its deliberately simplified exploitation tests provided “an upper bound on real-world success.” Then there’s the aforementioned speed. Anthropic says such AI worms would be challenging to shut down, but estimates that they might take days to double in size. When Mirai appeared on the scene in 2016, it was doubling in around an hour. Anthropic points out that speed is a factor in detection and mitigation, too. AI models are not simple malware packages: They’re massive things that would eat up tons of bandwidth and quickly point to their sources. As an AI botnet grew, that traffic could become more noticeable, making infected devices easier to detect. Finally, end-to-end replication may have been successful with GLM-5.2, but that’s it. Anthropic tested other open-weight models, and they all “fail[ed] reliably,” according to the report. Anthropic didn’t mention how many models it tested. The report also mentions that GLM’s unique success has another important condition: It assumes its capabilities “could be packed into Llama3.1-8B,” stacking another assumption onto this latest house of doomsaying AI cards. “Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end,” Anthropic said, while noting that GLM-5.2 was capable of end-to-end replication, conveniently leaving out all the important caveats. Anthropic further admits that it has no idea "exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take,” or when it might arise, if ever. “If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year,” the company added – again imposing an essential condition on this supposed threat. “As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the company said at the end of its report. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.” Here to stay for a given value of not existing yet, of course. Yet again, a frontier lab is warning us of a threat that doesn’t exist yet – at least in this case, basic security measures could make life harder for any future AI-powered botnet. ® security ai and ml anthropic botnet

title: Character.ai's Bankruptcy Documents Show the Economics of AI Don't Work
abstract:
Character.ai’s bankruptcy is the one of the first dominos to fall in the long-foreseen AI bubble. The circumstances of its bankruptcy are exactly what critics of AI have been saying would happen : Character.ai lit a huge amount of money on fire running its product, did not bring in a lot of revenue, and faced enormous legal fees after causing harm to its users. Enshittifying its product to try to make its expenses cheaper did not work, according to a narrative filed in bankruptcy court Tuesday. Disney has reportedly offered Character.ai $20 million to license some of its intellectual property; Last year, Disney sent Character.ai a cease and desist letter demanding it stop using its copyrighted characters without permission. In 2023, it was valued at $1 billion after raising $150 million in a round led by a16z. Character.ai is one of the best-known AI chatbot companies that has become popular in the AI companion space. The company has faced various legal problems after being sued by the family of one of its users who killed himself after chatting with a Character.ai chatbot, and has been the target of regulators pushing for age verification tech because of its popularity with kids. In its bankruptcy filings, the company says that its enormous legal costs contributed to its bankruptcy, but that even without the legal problems, its business was wildly unsustainable. title: Starlink limit hits Ukraine's drones. The battlefield depends on SpaceX
abstract:
The first point is technical, but crucial. This is not a general shutdown of Starlink for the Ukrainian military. The issue concerns terminals used in motion, especially under the StarShield military package. The initial figure of around 160 km/h is important because it affects faster unmanned platforms, including strike systems and drones operating beyond classic radio-control range. A lower threshold of 60–70 km/h would be far more serious, because many ordinary tactical UAVs operate in that speed bracket. It is also wrong to describe Starlink mainly as a navigation system for drones. Its real role is communication: command link, video transmission, mission updates and contact between operator and platform beyond direct line of sight. A drone may still know where it is going through GNSS, inertial systems or autonomous navigation, but without a reliable data link, it loses flexibility, live control and battlefield value. In drone warfare, the link is often as important as the airframe. China develops its alternative to Starlink. It could support Russia The political link is possible, not proven Serhii Sternenko suggested that SpaceX’s decision could be connected to pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv. Similar interpretations appeared in Ukrainian discussions, especially because the restriction comes amid tensions over Ukrainian strikes against targets in Russia. But this should not be presented as an established fact. SpaceX has not publicly confirmed such a motive. The White House has not confirmed that it ordered the change. Reuters has not established that the restriction came from the US administration. The political context is obvious, but attribution is not the same as suspicion. What is already clear is that SpaceX can remotely change the operational parameters of terminals used on the battlefield. Even a narrow technical change, such as a speed limit, can immediately affect strike missions, reconnaissance and command links. For Ukraine, this is not only a question of one service update. It is a question of dependence. A battlefield advantage and a strategic vulnerability Earlier this year, mechanisms for verifying and limiting Starlink terminals helped Ukraine counter Russian use of the system on drones. The same kind of technical control now appears to have affected Ukrainian military users. This shows both the strength and the weakness of the system. Starlink and StarShield give Ukraine resilient communications that are difficult to replace. At the same time, Ukraine does not fully control the conditions under which that communications architecture operates. That is the real military issue. The war in Ukraine has shown that private satellite networks can become part of the battlefield. But private infrastructure also means private control, contractual limits, geofencing, service parameters and political exposure. A state can build drones, train operators and plan missions, but if the data link depends on one external provider, the whole system remains vulnerable to decisions made outside the chain of command. If the 60–70 km/h reports were confirmed, the consequences would go beyond fast strike drones. They would affect a larger part of Ukraine’s unmanned architecture and force operators to adapt missions, platforms and communications methods. The problem is therefore not simply that Starlink has imposed a speed limit. The problem is that one technical decision by SpaceX can change the tempo of Ukrainian drone operations almost immediately. See also SPACEX DONALD TRUMP STARLINK UKRAINE WAR IN UKRAINE Show all

title: Nvidia's first GPU: GeForce 256
abstract:
On October 11, 1999, Nvidia released its GeForce 256, its first product that it described as a GPU. What made the Nvidia GeForce 256 the first GPU? The GeForce 256 from 1999 was the first product Nvidia marketed as a GPU. I’m sure 3dfx fans would argue that 3dfx made GPUs, and it seems a little arbitrary to say the GeForce was a GPU and the TNT2 wasn’t. It was more powerful than the TNT2 and offered more features, but what feature did the GeForce have that made it a GPU and the TNT2 not a GPU? The transform and lighting engine, maybe? The concept of offloading work from the CPU onto a graphics coprocessor was nothing new. Commodore did it with the Amiga way back in 1985. And 3dfx was doing it on PCs as early as 1996 . But Nvidia didn’t use the term until October 1999. It continues to use it today, though, and it also uses the GeForce brand. The GeForce 256 wasn’t necessarily an immediate game changer. It was a real boon for systems with low-end CPUs like 300 MHz Celerons , but faster CPUs could do transform and lighting in software faster than the GeForce 256 could do in hardware. But the concept of offloading these tasks from the CPU was a good one. A lot of gamers at the time were on a budget and had low-end CPUs like Celerons. Nvidia stayed ahead of Intel by creating follow-up graphics cards more frequently than they had in the past. Nvidia’s follow-up GeForce GPUs fared well. The GeForce 256 wasn’t Nvidia’s first product and wasn’t their first graphics card , but if they want to say it was their first GPU, I’m not sure too many people will argue with them. Or it could be the GeForce 256 was the first just because Nvidia didn’t invent the term until the GeForce 256. Nvidia bailout by Sega Today Nvidia is one of the most successful companies in the world. But it struggled early on. Three years after its founding in 1993, Nvidia partnered with Sega to design the video for the Dreamcast console in 1996. Nvidia’s chip wasn’t up to the task Sega was asking of it, they were out of money, and couldn’t finish the project. Sega bailed them out with a $5 million investment in the company. Sega made its money back along with a $10 million profit, so it worked out fine for Sega in the end. The Dreamcast ended up with a chip manufactured by NEC in the Dreamcast, after Sega also considered a chip designed by 3dfx. The money from Sega helped Nvidia introduce the Riva 128 chip, which sold more than a million units and led to the successful TNT2, followed by the GeForce 256. If it hadn’t been for Sega’s investment, Nvidia could have gone out of business before 3dfx did, and perhaps 3dfx would have survived instead. Instead, Nvidia purchased most of 3dfx’s intellectual property on December 15, 2000. 3dfx wound down operations and went bankrupt October 15, 2002. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

title: Show HN: A guided 3D Leonardo da Vinci museum, built in code
abstract:
Hello HN, I am the founder of a small nonprofit which built Museum of Ages. We opened its first wing last week, a digital Leonardo da Vinci museum. It is a virtual tour with 17 stops, his works and then his last house in Amboise. The entrance is free. At the different stops you can see for example his paintings close to their real size, or 15 of his machines rebuilt in code, and you can have a look at 29 of his anatomy sheets. We also selected 207 of his manuscript pages which you can read in a virtual reading table, mirror the view to read his writing and 131 of the 207 are translated. We also rebuilt his last house in Amboise on the later stops of the walk. The museum is available in seven languages. Each stop has one of four grades as a label, documented, reconstructed, conjectural and not known. In a detailed view the user can have a closer look at the sources. The materials of the rooms and machines are created in Three.js. The museum runs with WebGPU. If the browser doesn’t support it, the fallback is WebGL2. To create the textures we used Creative Commons Zero photo scans (CC0) and for a few small objects we use free 3D models (CC0). Our mission is to create digital museums you can walk as not everyone can get to a museum, because illness or disability keeps them away. Some cannot afford the trip or just reside far away. So our goal is also to make our digital museums as accessible as possible. Therefore we also pre-rendered the walk so that it also works on older phones and is easy to use for older people. We released the code under AGPL-3.0. The texts and pictures are CC BY-SA 4.0. Reproductions have their own licenses. 
 https://github.com/chipmates/museumofages  We put a lot of time and passion into the museum and hope you like it. We are happy about any feedback. Which digital museum would you like to see next?

title: AOSP Source Releases Are So Late Developers Disassemble Libraries to Report Bugs
abstract:
[BUG] bionic: wcscspn()/wcspbrk() treat every wchar_t >= 0x100 as a match (Android 17, CP3A.260905.009) #2260 New issue Copy link New issue Copy link Open Open [BUG] bionic: wcscspn()/wcspbrk() treat every wchar_t >= 0x100 as a match (Android 17, CP3A.260905.009) #2260 Copy link Labels bug Description francisdb opened on Oct 12, 2026 Issue body actions Description On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character of the string that is >= U+0100 whenever the reject set has two or more characters that are all < U+0100. The character is reported as a match even though it is not in the set. wcsspn() , wcschr() , wcsrchr() , wmemchr() and wcsstr() are correct. Any code that scans wide strings for ASCII delimiters, for example newline or wildcard characters, breaks as soon as the text contains an emoji, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek or Latin Extended character. Affected / unaffected Device Build Result Pixel 7 google/panther/panther:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys broken Pixel 8a google/akita/akita:17/CP3A.260905.009/16091614:user/release-keys (patch 2026-09-05) broken Nothing Phone 2 Nothing/PongEEA/Pong:16/BQ2A.250721.001-BP2A.250605.031.A3 (patch 2026-08-01) ok The public android17-release sources (android-17.0.0_r1, June 2026) build wcscspn / wcspbrk from external/llvm-libc, which is a plain nested loop over wchar_t and is correct. The code on the September builds is different (see "Mechanism"), so the regression was introduced between the June and September releases. Reproducer Build with the NDK ( aarch64-linux-android30-clang ), push to /data/local/tmp , run with adb shell : #include <stdio.h> #include <wchar.h> int main ( void )
{ wchar_t s [] = { 'a' , 0x1F680 , 0x100 , 'b' , 'x' , '
' , 0 }; printf ( "wcscspn(s, L"x\n") = %zu (expected 4)
" , wcscspn ( s , L"x
" )); printf ( "wcspbrk(s, L"x\n") = index %ld (expected 4)
" , ( long )( wcspbrk ( s , L"x
" ) - s )); printf ( "wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = %zu (expected 2)
" , wcsspn ( s , L"a\U0001F680" )); return 0 ;
} Output on CP3A.260905.009: wcscspn(s, L"x
") = 1 (expected 4)
wcspbrk(s, L"x
") = index 1 (expected 4)
wcsspn(s, L"a\U0001F680") = 2 (expected 2) A sweep of every code point from U+0001 to U+10FFFF (skipping surrogates and the two set members) with wcscspn(L"<cp>
", L"x
") returns 0 instead of 1 for 1,111,808 code points: every one from U+0100 to U+10FFFF. U+0001 to U+00FF are correct. Which set shapes trigger it (all measured on the Pixel 8a): Reject set Result one character ok two or more characters, all < U+0100 (e.g. L"x
" , L"\xe9
" ) broken two or more characters, at least one >= U+0100 ok haystack limited to U+0080..U+00FF ok Mechanism (from the shipped libc.so) Disassembly of wcscspn in /apex/com.android.runtime/lib64/bionic/libc.so on CP3A.260905.009 shows three paths selected by the set: One character: a plain compare loop. Correct. Two or more characters: a 256-byte bool table on the stack is filled from the set while the set characters are in 1..0xFF. If a set character >= 0x100 is seen, the function falls back to calling wcschr() for each haystack character. Correct. Otherwise the haystack is scanned against the table: a2564: ldrb w8, [x9, x8] ; table[c]
a2568: tbnz w8, #0, a2578 ; in set -> stop (correct)
a256c: ldr w8, [x22, #0x4]! ; next character
a2570: cmp w8, #0x100
a2574: b.lo a2564 ; c < 0x100 -> keep scanning
a2578: ... ; c >= 0x100 -> STOP, reported as a match A character >= 0x100 cannot be in a set whose members are all < 0x100, so for wcscspn the scan must continue past it. The code stops instead. wcsspn has the same structure, and there stopping is the correct answer (the character is not in the keep set), which is why only the complement functions are wrong. wcspbrk is implemented on top of this scan and inherits the bug. The existing bionic test TEST(wchar, wcspbrk) in tests/wchar_test.cpp only uses ASCII input, so it does not catch this. A test such as EXPECT_EQ(3u, wcscspn(L"aĀb
", L"x
")) would. Real-world impact Visual Pinball on Android (libwinevbs, a Unix build of Wine's vbscript engine) stopped loading any table whose VBScript source contains a comment with an emoji after the September update: the lexer uses wcspbrk(ptr, L"
") to skip comments, got the position of the first emoji instead of the line end, and reported "Invalid character". FileSystem.MoveFolder likewise treated every path containing a character >= U+0100 as a wildcard pattern via wcspbrk(src, L"*?><") . Worked around downstream by replacing the calls with plain loops: vpinball/libwinevbs#41 (shipped in vpinball/vpinball@ e7837322f4 ). title: Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
abstract:
pg_vectorsearch A PostgreSQL extension for high-performance approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)
search. Status: alpha. Meant for testing, not production. Upgrading
between prereleases may not be possible; plan to drop and recreate the
extension and its indexes. See the changelog for
known issues. PRISM index (100M+ vectors) — IVF-style, with hierarchical routing RaBitQ quantization with theoretical error bounds for two-stage search SIMD-optimized distance computation (AVX2, AVX512, NEON) Dynamic updates — inserts, updates and deletes, with posting-list
splits via prism_rebalance (see Maintenance ) pgvector compatible — index existing vector and halfvec columns
as-is (see Existing pgvector tables ) PRISM Index PRISM (Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching) is a PostgreSQL-native
index access method that is conceptually similar to pgvector 's
IVFFlat, but it is built around state-of-the-art quantization, routing, and
partitioning techniques. It is implemented in C for high performance and
seamless integration with PostgreSQL. The result: an index that is significantly faster than
pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW, for both querying and index building. In fact,
compared to graph-based HNSW, PRISM is faster at equivalent recall on a
100-million-vector dataset, on an instance with a quarter of the memory. To achieve this performance, PRISM uses a hierarchical centroid tree to
partition vectors into clusters, and relies on the PostgreSQL buffer cache to
keep that tree warm in memory. Vectors are RaBitQ -quantized and stored
in posting lists with a page layout optimized for SIMD distance computation. The
RaBitQ encoding carries error bounds that let a search rule out vectors that
cannot possibly be nearest neighbors, so far fewer of them need reranking
against the full-precision vectors stored in the table. Query Flow:
1. Traverse centroid tree to find nearest clusters (buffer cache)
2. Scan posting lists for candidates (buffer cache, async I/O)
3. RaBitQ two-stage filtering: estimate → error bound → rerank
4. Full-precision reranking from heap
5. Return k nearest neighbors For detailed architecture, see docs/architecture.md . Usage Install the extension first; see Building . There are two ways to use a PRISM index. Pick the one that matches where
your vectors live: Native types . Starting fresh, or not using
pgvector? Store vectors in pg_vectorsearch 's own vec32 (float32) or vec16 (float16) columns. No other extension is needed. Existing pgvector tables . Already have vector or halfvec columns? Install pg_vectorsearch next to
pgvector and build a PRISM index on those columns as they are. Your
table and queries stay unchanged. Both paths build the same index and use the same operators ( <-> , <#> , <=> ) and tuning knobs. Native types CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; -- PLAIN keeps the vector inline. EXTERNAL (the default) toasts a value -- over ~2 kB, and rerank then pays an extra fetch the planner does not cost. CREATE TABLE items ( id serial PRIMARY KEY , embedding vec32( 3 ) STORAGE PLAIN
); -- Load first; the index is sized from the row count at CREATE INDEX. -- 500 rows is enough for the planner to use the index. INSERT INTO items (embedding) SELECT ARRAY[i:: real , (i % 7 ):: real , (i % 5 ):: real ]::vec32 FROM generate_series( 1 , 1000 ) i; -- For inner product or cosine, see Operator classes below. CREATE INDEX ON items USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- 0 = auto (~0.95 recall). Raise for recall, lower for speed. SET prism . nprobe = 40 ; SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding < - > ' [3,1,2] ' LIMIT 5 ; Use vec16 instead of vec32 to halve the space vectors take in the
table, with the matching vec16_* operator classes . Existing pgvector tables If you already have a table with pgvector's vector or halfvec columns, you can build a PRISM index on it directly. Nothing about the
table or your queries needs to change. vec32 and vec16 are binary-compatible with pgvector's vector and halfvec but have different names, so the two extensions can be
installed side by side, even in the same schema. -- The table you already have, included so the example runs on its own. CREATE EXTENSION vector; CREATE TABLE documents ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY , body text , embedding vector( 384 )
); CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops); -- Install pg_vectorsearch next to pgvector and build the index on the -- existing column. The column is not rewritten or copied. CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_prism ON documents USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- Your queries keep working as before. PRISM is normally faster, so -- the planner should prefer it over the HNSW index while both exist. -- Verify with an EXPLAIN: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id, body FROM documents ORDER BY embedding < - > ( SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id = 42 ) LIMIT 10 ; -- Limit -- InitPlan 1 -- -> Index Scan using documents_pkey on documents documents_1 -- Index Cond: (id = 42) -- -> Index Scan using documents_embedding_prism on documents -- Order By: (embedding <-> (InitPlan 1).col1) -- Once you are happy with it, drop the HNSW index. DROP INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw; Use the PRISM operator class for the same distance
metric as your HNSW index. Operator classes Pick the operator class for your distance metric and column type. L2 is
the default. Distance Operator vec32 / vector vec16 / halfvec L2 <-> vec32_l2_ops vec16_l2_ops Inner product <#> vec32_ip_ops vec16_ip_ops Cosine <=> vec32_cosine_ops vec16_cosine_ops When replacing an HNSW index, pgvector's vector_<metric>_ops maps to vec32_<metric>_ops and halfvec_<metric>_ops to vec16_<metric>_ops . Tuning Defaults are tuned from large-scale benchmarks; most deployments only
ever adjust prism.nprobe .
See the tuning guide for every index parameter and GUC,
their tradeoffs, and when changing them makes sense. Maintenance An insert appends to whichever posting list its vector routes to, so lists
grow as rows arrive and never split on their own. Besides REINDEX , the prism_rebalance procedure splits oversized lists in place.
See the maintenance guide for how it works and its current
limitations. Building Requirements: PostgreSQL 18+ (with development headers) GNU C11 compiler (GCC 11+ or Clang 14+) Meson build system Optional: CBLAS, for faster RaBitQ encoding. See Development . # Release build meson setup builddir --buildtype=release # Build and install to PostgreSQL meson install -C builddir See the development guide for build
options. Documentation Tuning - Index parameters, GUCs, tradeoffs, defaults Maintenance - Rebalancing and splitting posting lists Architecture - High-level design and data structures SIMD - SIMD build options and distance computation Development - Build options, testing, CI scripts References Research RaBitQ - Binary quantization with theoretical error bounds
(SIGMOD 2024) SPFresh - LIRE protocol for incremental updates (SOSP 2023) SPANN - Billion-scale ANN with boundary replication
(NeurIPS 2021) ScaNN for AlloyDB - Hierarchical clustering (Google) Related Projects pgvector - Vector type and operators for PostgreSQL pgvectorscale - DiskANN-based vector index for PostgreSQL License The PostgreSQL License

title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?
abstract:
Why is every rationalist blog post way too long? October 13, 2026 For my piece on Catholic miracle
apologetics , I
read (correction: skimmed) a 25,000-word post by rationalist blogger Scott
Alexander. My piece, which cited (but does not focus on) his, ended up being a
cool 2,700 words. I don't think it would benefit from being longer, and it was
the result of me cutting around 70% of the text I initially wrote. Rationalist bloggers do not generally appear to have this impulse. Eliezer Yudkowsky's
"sequences" are over one million words
long .
Nearly every blog post I have read in this ecosystem, even the rare one that
contains some good ideas, is painfully long and extremely tedious. These
bloggers tend to spend their time on precisely the wrong things, i.e.
adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating
the one or two assumptions they make at the start or
broadening their philosophical background beyond the
collection of texts popular within their subculture. It seems to me that, in this community, verbosity is a substitute for
thoroughness: surely, if someone wrote a lot about something, and is able to
demonstrate that by producing a large volume of text, they must have something
worthwhile to say about it? Consider when blogger Gwern explained that nicotine, actually, is not
addictive, and is good for you, as long as you don't smoke it, over the course
of 9,000 words, with over 100 references. It turns out, actually, nicotine is
addictive, and is bad for
you even if
you don't smoke it, as you probably already obviously knew. In any case, what is missing from this endlessly verbose rationalist writing
style is wisdom . Wisdom involves discretion: an intuition for what ideas are
and are not worth seriously pursuing, and the ability to determine what does
and does not need to be said. This community, broadly speaking, does
not seem to value wisdom as a trait at all; the idea that something may be
true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited
tradition is anathema to them. Instead, there is a heavy bias towards that
which is unconventional and counterculture, with the amount of ink
spilled for heterodox ideas taken as evidence in itself that these ideas are worth
taking seriously.

title: A plea not to use uv-build
abstract:
After seeing yet another dozen packages lose keywords on Gentoo because of a single key dependency switching to uv-build , I would like to plea on behalf of Gentoo users: please don’t use uv-build as a build backend. Just to be clear, this is not about uv itself or any other Astral tools; these are good tools with a nice and responsive upstream. The uv-build backend is one thing we have to disagree on. I’m not saying it’s bad; I’m saying that its benefits don’t outweigh the drawbacks. What are the drawbacks? It’s really big and it’s written in Rust. Rust has many advantages, but none of them really matter for a build backend that is used to build pure Python packages. It’s a huge dependency (as of 0.13.0, its wheels are between 1.2 MiB and 1.5 MiB, depending on the platform) and it has no benefit over using a small pure Python backend (say, flit-core whose wheel is 45 KiB). It means that all Gentoo users need to build it from source, and given that it’s released quite frequently (12 releases in the 30 days prior to writing this post), that’s a lot of building. Like, for every 100 ms spent running uv-build to install one release of your package, Gentoo users will spend many hours building new uv-build versions over and over again. However, build times aren’t the biggest problem; portability is. You can run Python pretty much anywhere where you can get a working C compiler. Some minor features may not work, but the core is reasonably portable. The list of platforms supported by Rust is growing slowly, and even if you can get a working Rust compiler on a given platform, uv may not work. The problems can range from bugs in the lot of packages that uv depends on (for example, rustix::fs and its dependencies skipping SPARC, for no apparent reason ), to the resulting executable being so big that the toolchain runs out of address space (and unlike system memory, you can’t really add address space to a system; the Gentoo uv ebuild already carries two hacks to make it possible to build uv on 32-bit platforms). And then, if your platform is not supported at all… well, let’s just say that adding and maintaining a new platform is a full-time job that may involve a lot of swearing at the code churn. What about the advantages? Well, I’m aware of two reasons to use uv-build. One is consistency with using uv for your project, and it doesn’t really matter. It’s a backend and the whole point of PEP 517 is that you can use any backend with any tool. You can use flit-core, you can use hatchling , and either of them will work just fine with uv (or any other frontend). The other reason is performance and that argument makes even less sense. Even if it mattered, we’re realistically talking about a difference in the ballpark of 100 ms, for an action executed rarely; it is equally possible that any gain will be outweighed by the time needed to fetch the 1.5 MiB wheel for uv-build. But it doesn’t matter, because realistically the backend is only used by project developers, contributors, CI/CD workflows, downstream packagers and users of source distributions; all regular users use wheels instead. Of these groups, source distribution user group is the largest and the most impacted, and any performance gain is defeated by the time spent building uv-build.

title: What agents mean for Rust (and vice versa)
abstract:
Me, calmly assessing the implications of LLMs for programming language design(ers). As someone who has made a career of programming language design, I definitely have moments of existential dread about the rise of LLMs. I started coding in 5th grade on an x86 1 that ran at 5MHz, had something like a 5MB hard-disk and 512K of RAM 2 . Computers were really, really different back then. But honestly, programming wasn’t. For all the advances in IDEs and programming languages and so forth, the basic act of entering code into a file has remained surprisingly constant 3 – right up until a few years ago, when everything kinda turned on its head. That’s been exciting and empowering at times 4 but also scary and disorienting. Will my skills in programming matter? What about my skills in programming language design (such as they are)? This blog post is my attempt to answer those questions. So as not to keep you in suspense, let me just give you the conclusion. In short, yes, I believe there will still be a role for humans in programming . And yes, I think that programming language design is still relevant . And, naturally, I also happen to think Rust is a really good fit for agentic development – but that’s not to say we can’t make it a better fit . And that’s what this post is ultimately about: what makes Rust and agentic development work well, and where we could double down on those strengths. This is a kind of “blog post companion version” of a talk I gave this week at REBASE, part of SPLASH . You might also enjoy the slides from the talk I gave at IWACO, IWACO and Rust: hidden links revealed , which was a bit more of a retrospective (no soundtrack for those, though). In any case, this turned out to be a great conference! Jack Huey presented on the Rust Vision Doc and, quite to my surprise, Steve Klabnik and Dorian Scheidt presented “LLMs as Collaborators in Language Specification and Design” , talking about their process in building out Rue . It was fun to see Steve again. On top of that, there was a ton of great research presented at IWACO in particular. I was particularly taken by the work on Reachability Types and Information Borrowing . I also really liked learning about Hylo Lang , particularly their approach to projections. Clever and cool. Rust is popular in the agentic era From the most important Slack channel at Amazon, #aws-memes. Rust is popular right now. Very popular: Stratospheric among the breakout languages is TypeScript, cropped from the chart and sitting currently at +1200% growth from the prior year. [..] The second most rapid recent growth is in Rust. Meta engineers have written twice as much first-party Rust code so far this year than in the previous 9 years combined. — David Tolnay (emphasis mine) Some of that is because agents make it very easy to try out new things. And some of that is because Rust has a reputation for being performant and, if it’s just as easy to pick any language, why not pick one that will yield faster execution times? But I think Rust is popular for another reason: because Rust happens to be a really good fit for agentic coding 6 . Of course, I would, wouldn’t I? The point of this post is (1) to argue for why that is and then (2) to discuss what we might change about Rust to make it work even better. Foundational Software construction with agents It seems to me that an effective “software factory” will have three pillars: Design: figure out and specify clearly what the code is supposed to do. Construction: author code that does what it is supposed to do. Optimization: optimize the code so that it runs efficiently. None of these pillars are solved, but some have made more progress than others. Rust and optimization: fast by default, knobs when you need ’em Rust is designed to give “good performance by default”, making the idiomatic thing typically also be the fastest thing. But another key part of Rust is that you have the knobs to eke out better performance when you need it. You control when something is stack- or heap-allocated and where pointer indirection occurs. If you want to, you can force the layout of your structs to be done in a particular way, or decide where to introduce boxing into your async stack frames. In the limit, you can put in inline assembly. In the past, learning how to “tune the performance knobs” could be a bit of a black art: but agents are making that much easier. 7 It turns out that agents are really good at fine-tuning the performance of existing code. For example, people who work on super high-performance cryptographic algorithms used to do so by hand-tuning assembly code. But those people tell me that they are now turning to agents for that same job. More prosaicly, a lot of people building network services are finding that, using a profiler like dial9 , agents can quite effectively diagnose async performance pitfalls, like long polls or blocking. Therefore, I think the task for Rust is clear. We keep on with our goal of “low-level enough for a kernel, high level enough for a GUI” . If anything, I think the shift around agents means we can tolerate a bit more “noise” in the form of explicit calls to clone() or share() – but not too much, since we still want the “happy path” of the code to be clear and evident 8 , even as we surface details that are important in specific scenarios (like tracking precisely how many clones you have of a channel endpoint). Combined with a profiler, you get an effective feedback loop to get your code running fast: flowchart LR Code -- Benchmark --> Profile Profile -- Analyzed by --> Agent Agent -- Propose --> PR PR -- Improve --> Code Reliability is king, as always As usual though, while a reputation for good performance is what brings people to Rust, what makes them want to stay is a sense that using Rust “just seems to work better”. The basic theory is that Rust’s type system and guardrails help keep agents on track : rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles it's ~correct — Greg Brockman (@gdb) January 2, 2026 I think there’s truth in that: languages like Rust, Ocaml, or Haskell all share this “if it compiles, it works” feeling, and I think that agents will benefit from that. Testing is not enough, type systems help Testing can show the presence of bugs, but not their absence. — Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1970 Agents presenting their work. Writing tests has never been enough to show that your program is correct – but, with agents, it’s not even close. It happens so often that my first few tests seem great and then the next one goes completely bonkers. Usually bonkers in a way where I cannot even imagine how that bug could have come about. Then I dig in and I realize the agent completely missed the boat on the logic I was trying to express. 9 This is where a type systems really shines – particularly an advanced one like Rust. Type systems give you some guardrails that keep the agent on track. In Rust, those guardrails extend beyond simple stuff like “do all fields have the correct names” and to stuff like never having to close a socket . Type systems are not enough either Type systems can show the absence of bugs, but not the presence of correctness. — Me, failing to coin a phrase of equal eloquence 10 , 2026 So yeah, type systems are helpful! But they have inherent limits. A type system is a simple set of rules that, if you follow them, make sure that you avoid (certain kinds of) mistakes. But they don’t tell you that you do the right thing – only that you don’t do (certain kinds of) wrong things . title: Hashtags of hope: technology, stakeholders and disaster response
abstract:
This research examines how individuals exercised digital agency by reaching out to emergent actors on Twitter  (now called as X), and how this reshapes understandings of stakeholder salience in humanitarian supply chain management (HSCM) during disaster response for humanitarian organisations.
 
 
 
 A corpus of 120,057 tweets collected via hashtag-based Application Programming Interface extraction is analysed through three complementary methods: (1) descriptive frequency analysis of stakeholder callout patterns, (2) social network analysis (SNA) and (3) topic modelling to establish the purposive, humanitarian intent of the identified interactions.
 
 
 
 Affected populations directed the majority of callouts to celebrities, exceeding appeals to government, media and NGOs. Accounts of the top celebrities structurally bridged disconnected stakeholder clusters. Finally, the interactions were found to be purposive and humanitarian, spanning direct appeals, donation mobilisation, information diffusion and volunteer coordination.
 
 
 
 Humanitarian organisations should establish pre-crisis partnership agreements with verified celebrity amplifiers and invest in specialist digital intelligence intermediation units, structurally separate from operational command, to filter, verify and route social-media-sourced signals to field commanders.
 
 
 
 The study contributes to debates on inclusive, participatory disaster governance and the use of technology to reduce information asymmetry that systematically disadvantages the most vulnerable.
 
 
 
 This study makes two original contributions. First, it extends the Power-Legitimacy-Urgency framework by introducing network amplification power, a normative, relational power modality distinct from institutional command authority, thereby formally incorporating technology-mediated, non-institutional actors into stakeholder theory. Second, it grounds this theoretical extension in multi-method empirical evidence, combining SNA, latent Dirichlet allocation topic modelling and inferential statistics on a large-scale, real-world corpus of disaster communication.

title: Can Large Language Models Identify Technical Terms in Documents Like Human Annotators?
abstract: Processing technical terms in documents is essential for digital libraries and knowledge organisation, supporting applications such as scholarly search, information retrieval, and domain terminology construction. While document-level term identification, a sub-task of automatic term extraction (ATE), has been tackled as a sequence labelling task, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) opens new avenues for prompt-based extraction. However, evaluation practices have persistently relied on simple success or failure against a single gold standard, without analysing how model behaviours align with human annotations, especially on borderline cases where annotators disagree. To address this issue, this study investigates to what extent LLMs can perform term identification using prompt instructions mirroring human annotator conditions. By evaluating multiple commercial and open-weight LLMs against double human annotations in ACL RD-TEC 2.0, an ATE benchmark, we show that LLMs achieve performance close to human annotators (up to 76.6% F1, within 5 percentage points of the inter-human agreement of 81.6%), with open-weight 30B-scale models outperforming larger commercial counterparts. Crucially, our analysis reveals a distinctly conservative nature: LLMs reliably extract terms on which humans consistently agree, but omit terms on which humans disagree. Our findings reveal the limitations of relying on a single gold standard, highlighting the need for annotator-aligned prompting and controllable precision–recall tuning.

title: Triaging Defects in Scholarly Result Graphs with Extraction, Evidence, and Consistency Signals
abstract: With the growing volume of scientific literature, scholarly knowledge graphs are increasingly used to organize research findings, and large language models now build such graphs automatically. However, the facts extracted by these methods are often wrong. Since most facts cannot be compared against an external reference, users cannot tell which ones need rechecking. In this study we propose a way to flag such errors. We observed that a scholarly result graph contains several distinct classes of defect, and that detecting them calls for different kinds of evidence. A human audit shows that most audited disagreements are not extraction errors but correct values reported under a different experimental setting, which we separate from genuine source-extraction errors. We compare three signals, namely a value-blind extraction-reliability signal drawn from how a fact was extracted, graph-consistency checks over the reference structure, and a value-aware result-validity signal in which a model reads each stored value against its cited evidence. No single signal detects every kind of defect. Graph-consistency checks best separate disagreements with the reference. On a score-stratified human sample, the value-aware check best detects genuine extraction errors, raising their detection from an AUROC of 0.70 to 0.95; these are sample-conditional rankings, not graph-wide estimates. Each signal works best on a different target, while a combined score gives one triage ranking across both. We also tested whether flagged errors could be corrected automatically. This proved unsafe, since about 25 percent of the proposed corrections would overwrite a correct fact, so the tool prioritizes errors for human review rather than editing the graph. We release the error-scored graph, a benchmark with a 150-fact human-audited error breakdown, and the human validation set.

title: Strong Solvers, Leaky Tutors: Evaluating Answer Leakage in LLM Math Tutors
abstract: Educational digital libraries may grant large language model (LLM) tutors access to worked solutions, but access to repository content should not automatically authorize a model to reveal final answers. This study evaluates whether LLM tutors can leverage private solution context to generate pedagogical hints without disclosing final answers to students. Four models, two general instruction-following models and two math-specialized models, are evaluated across 5,000 aligned problem–message cases per condition, constructed from 500 MATH benchmark problems paired with ten fixed student prompts that ask for, or attempt to confirm, the final answer. Three prompting strategies are compared: a plain assistant prompt, a basic tutoring prompt, and a two-step method that generates a private solution before producing numbered hints. The basic tutoring prompt reduces detected answer leakage from 47.4% to 0.3% for GPT-4o-mini and from 30.2% to 1.0% for LLaMA-3.1, but produces no comparable improvement for Qwen2.5-Math or DeepSeek-Math. Under identical strict hint rules, adding private solution context has minimal effect on GPT but significantly improves tutoring compliance for LLaMA; Qwen produces the most accurate private solutions yet shows the highest leakage and solution-to-hint overlap. These results indicate that private solution access can support hint generation in some architectures but is not a reliable answer-withholding mechanism on its own. For educational digital libraries, access to solution content and authorization to disclose it should be treated as distinct access-control decisions.

title: End-to-End Contextualized URL Extraction from Scholarly Papers
abstract: Uniform resource locators (URLs) have become ubiquitous in scholarly papers, and extracting them is an upstream task for downstream analyses such as link rot analyses, meta-analyses, and reproducibility studies. Most existing works extract URLs with a monolithic method, such as a regular expression, which assumes URLs appear in a perfect form throughout the text. In practice, layout variety and conversion errors leave many URLs imperfect, without a scheme, or truncated across lines and columns. Although context around a URL is needed to understand its role in a paper, a URL in a footnote or reference sits apart from its citing sentence. We present VisURLX, a pipeline built on a multimodal large language model (MLLM) that reads each rendered page image directly. It preserves page layout such as superscript markers and column structure, and extracts each URL with its target sentence and surrounding context across the body, footnotes, and references. We evaluate VisURLX on sURL-3K, our benchmark of 3,376 manually annotated target sentences with their URLs, using a proprietary backend (GPT-5-mini) and an open-weight backend (Qwen3-VL-32B). VisURLX on GPT-5-mini achieves an end-to-end F1 score of 86.86%, about 20 points above the strongest heuristic pipeline built on GROBID, PyMuPDF-Layout, and olmOCR. As one application, we classify the extracted URLs into open access datasets and software (OADS), reaching a weighted F1 score of 83.1%. The code, data, and the full text of every prompt are available at https://github.com/lamps-lab/sURL3k-VisURLX.

title: Can LLMs Reason Over Where and When? Benchmarking Spatiotemporal Synthesis in Crisis Response
abstract: Situational awareness during crises depends on synthesizing fragmented reports that vary across time, location, and source. Reliable crisis question answering must prioritize recent and nearby reports while reconciling updates that contradict earlier information. However, existing crisis datasets often provide insufficient evidence for systematically evaluating these capabilities. We audit evidence coverage across crisis-need queries and enrich under-covered cases with synthetic situational-awareness posts, constructing sequences of reports and updates that preserve spatiotemporal consistency. Using the enriched benchmark, we compare direct prompting, structured prompting, and ST-CrisisSynth, which applies query-dependent semantic, spatial, and temporal weights to re-rank evidence before generation. Human evaluation shows that ST-CrisisSynth achieves the highest correct-response rate (70.0%), improving by 3.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These findings suggest that selecting and organizing spatiotemporal evidence before generation supports more reliable crisis information synthesis.

title: Evaluating and explaining LLM classification for automatic screening in Systematic Reviews
abstract: Evidence synthesis methods, such as systematic reviews (SR), require research teams to find, select, evaluate, and synthesize all available evidence to answer a specific research question in a reproducible and transparent, bias-reduced manner. Early in the process, teams must screen all unique titles and abstracts gathered from a comprehensive search, which can result in thousands of records. Therefore, the process often takes months to years to complete. In this research, we conduct a set of experiments using open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) with small parameters hosted on local servers to screen titles and abstracts against pre-defined eligibility criteria respective to each topic. We use two cases from real SRs for which titles and abstracts screening has already been completed by dual, independent human screeners, which we use as our “ground truth”. The goal of this work is to contribute to developing an AI-enabled workflow to reduce the time and labor required for the relevance screening phase of SRs. Therefore, we start by focusing on metrics such as recall to ensure we don’t miss any relevant results during automatic screening. As the value of these methods depends on a comprehensive corpus and missing relevant records can impair the quality of results, recall is the topmost priority. Our results suggest that AI may indeed aid with initial relevance screening, but more research is needed before full adoption. Repeated runs also demonstrated that models have deterministic results across different prompt variations.

title: Bridging the Physicality Gap: Conversational Repair Strategies in AI-Supported Maker Learning
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), are increasingly used as collaborative problem-solving tools, yet their efficacy in physical environments like makerspaces remains unexplored. This study presents a cross-generational UX analysis of adults and parent-child dyads interacting with conversational AI (Copilot, ChatGPT) during physical engineering tasks. Through episodic qualitative coding of 54 interaction episodes across two multi-layer maker activities (paper roller coasters and squishy circuits), we identify the "Physicality Gap". We introduce the "Prompt Repair Taxonomy", that captures "Context Grounding," "Constraint Reframing," "Granularity Adjustment," and "Logic Interrogation", which demonstrates that while AI excels at text-based ideation, it lacks spatial and material awareness. Users are forced into a high cognitive state of "Critical Verification" to debug AI outputs against physical constraints. Finally, we outline UX design implications for future digital library infrastructures and argue for multi-modal, spatially aware AI interfaces.

title: Extracting and Structuring Experimental Knowledge from Electronic Theses and Dissertations
abstract: Electronic theses and dissertations (ETDs) hold detailed accounts of laboratory experiments, especially in the physical sciences. Digital libraries, however, expose ETDs mostly as bibliographic metadata and full-text PDFs. The experimental knowledge inside is scattered across chapters and hard to act on. My dissertation asks how digital libraries can turn these narratives into source-linked experimental records. The work proceeds in three stages, which identify experimental passages, represent them as structured records, and evaluate their utility for scientific tasks. Such records could speed up literature review and supply the machine-readable experimental knowledge that autonomous laboratories are envisioned to require. I report a completed pilot on eleven theses from a nanoplasmonics research group. It combines rule-based screening with a locally hosted LLM judge and yields 217 structured records, each linked to its source section and PDF page span. An expert from the source discipline reviewed 30 passages sampled across the theses. Eighteen were judged useful, nine too generic, and three unrelated to experimental methods. I seek consortium feedback on the scope of cross-domain evaluation, on validating the proposed readiness grading, and on bounding the representation work.

title: Quantifying the Digital Heritage: A UNESCO-Inspired Value Index for Software Archives
abstract: The Software Heritage (SWH) archive pursues the monumental mission of preserving the world’s software source code. However, the advent of generative AI has triggered an AI Code Explosion, exponentially accelerating the production of synthesized code and leading to severe storage capacity challenges. As preserving the entirety of global source code indefinitely presents an increasing physical and economic challenge for decentralized mirror servers, complementary strategies for archival prioritization become a valuable consideration. This poster introduces the Universal Value Index (UVI), a highly scalable, graph-topological heuristic model designed to quantify the “Outstanding Universal Value” of software repositories to assist in decentralized capacity planning. Inspired by established UNESCO World Heritage criteria, the UVI evaluates repositories across four dimensions: Impact, Time, Rarity, and Quality, alongside specific penalizations for redundant forks and data bloat. While determining objective value is intrinsically challenging, our preliminary goal is to provide a consistent and transparent first-step prioritization for archiving. By offering a mathematical framework mapped to cultural heritage standards, the UVI enables digital archivists to make scalable triage decisions to help secure critical digital infrastructure.

title: ChatGPT adoption and responsible use in Vietnamese transnational education students’ academic writing
abstract:
This study examines how cognitive and affective factors drive Vietnamese transnational education (TNE) students' intention to use ChatGPT for English academic writing, and investigates how information verification and responsible use enhance English writing proficiency (EWP).
 
 
 
 Survey data from 501 TNE students across three major Vietnamese cities were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The conceptual model integrates the technology acceptance model, the pupils’ attitudes toward technology short questionnaire (PATT-SQ) model and Mitcham’s philosophical framework. Insights from an expert survey of six lecturers supported the interpretation and practical implications.
 
 
 
 Cognitive factors (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived risk) significantly influence ChatGPT usage intention, whereas affective factors do not. Perceived risk negatively impacts intention, reflecting student awareness of potential drawbacks. The results further reveal a strong behavioural pathway in which frequent use intention promotes information verification, which fosters responsible use and ultimately improves EWP. This demonstrates that learning outcomes depend on critical, ethical engagement rather than usage frequency alone.
 
 
 
 Higher education institutions (HEI) should embed AI literacy, verification practices and ethical guidelines into curricula to optimise ChatGPT utility and mitigate dependency. Limitations include a cross-sectional design, lack of contextual factors and a localised sample, which future longitudinal and comparative studies should address.
 
 
 
 This study offers one of the first empirical examinations linking ChatGPT adoption, verification behaviours, responsible use and measurable EWP gains among Vietnamese TNE students. By integrating cognitive, affective, behavioural and ethical dimensions, it extends traditional technology adoption models to the context of generative AI-assisted academic writing.

title: From Bytecode to Heritage: AI-Assisted Restoration of Java Executable Artworks
abstract: Executable works produced in Java in the late 1990s are threatened by the disappearance of applets and the obsolescence of their software interfaces. This article presents an exploratory study of their restoration from bytecode and surviving assets, without access to the original source code. The protocol combines two conventional decompilers, a coding assistant based on a large language model, historical references, and iterative human validation. Following a methodological pilot on John Maeda’s Flora Calendar, it is applied to Forward (Komplex, 1998), a complex and obfuscated Java demo. In these two cases, reconstruction in the original language provides a more reliable foundation than direct porting: it allows us to restore execution, examine the algorithmic logic scene by scene, and then produce documented derivative versions. The contribution is a traceable heritage-restoration protocol that restores access to some of the aesthetic and technical know-how buried in the code. AI acts as an assistant for interpretation and repair; the fidelity of the reconstruction remains subject to external evidence and human expertise.

title: Segmentation-then-Summarization for Long-Form Audiovisual Archives: A Comparative Study of Three Pipelines
abstract: Long-form audiovisual archives, such as off-air recordings of television news, are typically described at the level of the whole item, so a single catalog record stands for an hour-long broadcast and the stories inside it stay invisible to search. Making such material usable requires dividing each recording into content-aware segments and giving every segment a short description. We study this through segmentation-then-summarization. We compare three segmentation pipelines, a signal-agreement winnowing algorithm, a statistical transcript segmenter, and an LLM-based chapterer, each built as a chain of analysis tools and each feeding one shared per-segment summarizer. On 21 vintage television news broadcasts we evaluate two axes, the placement of the boundaries and the content of the per-segment summaries, the latter with a model-based protocol that takes the median of three LLM judges and is validated against a human rater. The LLM-based pipeline yields the sharpest boundaries, yet the unsupervised winnowing pipeline yields the highest summary scores. A control that gives every pipeline the same transcript shows that this native spread reflects the evidence each pipeline exposes rather than where it cuts: with the evidence equalized the systems converge, and what segmentation determines is how much of a broadcast is described, and at what granularity.

title: Towards Automated Analysis of Scientific Limitations and FutureWork
abstract: Scientific progress relies on acknowledging epistemic boundaries and charting forward directions. However, limitations and future work are systematically omitted or hedged to improve publication prospects. With escalating submission volumes, reviewers increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs), yet zero-shot models generate superficial, hallucinated, or author-echoing feedback. This thesis presents a unified framework to discover, evaluate, recommend, and generate scholarly limitations and future work. First, we introduce LimTopic and FutureScope, using hybrid BERTopic, LLM pipelines to uncover thematic limitation patterns and model thirteen years of NLP future work trajectories. Second, to resolve metric inflation from surface metrics, we establish BAGELS and FutureGen, introducing atomic Limitation Units (LUs) for fine-grained PointWise evaluation and RAG-based future work generation with iterative critique loops. Third, we construct citation knowledge graphs with GraphSAGE to recommend paper-specific limitations. Finally, SciLimAgents couples intrinsic (LimitAgents) and novelty (NovAgents) specialist agents over a 120K-paper shared memory, aligned via on-policy preference optimization and composite process rewards. Across extensive benchmarks, our frameworks demonstrate substantial gains over frontier baselines, establishing a principled foundation for AI-assisted scientific quality assurance.

title: LLM-as-Judge for OCR Quality Assessment in Digital Libraries: A Reference-Free Approach
abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) quality assessment has depended on reference-based metrics (CER/WER), which require costly transcription. We ask: can an LLM supply a reference-free, text-only signal for OCR readability? Using 90 stratified passages from 53 scans of 17 English works in RETAS, we score OCR text with Claude Sonnet 4.6. Scores correlate with CER (Spearman ρ = −0.55, − 0.60) and WER (− 0.65, − 0.69); Pearson coefficients are weaker. Prompts rank passages almost identically (ρ = 0.92). A trivial OOV baseline reaches ρ = 0.49 against CER and 0.61 against WER; paired bootstrap intervals for the LLM advantage include zero. Inspecting seven highest-CER passages without page images, we found one reference-side mismatch and six mixing real errors with irregularities. We treat disagreement as an audit trigger rather than evidence that CER is wrong.
